=========== P1 proof
# Proof of P1

Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.

## Existence and evaluation of the density

For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
\[
\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
\tag{1}
\]
where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
\[
n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
\[
Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
\tag{2}
\]
Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).

The series
\[
D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
\tag{3}
\]
converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
\[
x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
\[
|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
\qquad x\geq1.
\tag{5}
\]
Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).

We will use the elementary Euler identity
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
\tag{6}
\]
To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).

For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
\[
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).

If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
\[
g(q,l)=\frac cq
\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
\tag{8}
\]
Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
\[
0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
\tag{9}
\]

## The finite second-moment identity

Let
\[
L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
\]
The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
\[
L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
\tag{10}
\]
These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.

For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
\[
b_{p,t}(l)=
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
\[
qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
\tag{11}
\]
For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
The last equality uses
\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).

The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]

## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates

The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
\[
r=ab^2,
\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
\tag{15}
\]
For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
\[
A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
\]
The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
\[
L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
\[
0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
\leq3c^2<\infty,
\tag{17}
\]
where the two series are bounded by
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.

We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
\[
1+L(p)+L(p^2)
=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
\]
Consequently (6) implies
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
\tag{18}
\]

For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
\[
\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
\tag{19}
\]
For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]
For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
\[
\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
\tag{21}
\]

Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).

For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.

## The Ramanujan series

There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
\[
|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
\tag{23}
\]
This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).

For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
\[
\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
\]
Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
\[
c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
\tag{24}
\]

The finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
\]
Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
\[
c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
\]
Adding these two exact identities yields
\[
c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
\tag{25}
\]
By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
=c^2\prod_p
\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
\tag{26}
\]
Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
=1-\frac2{p^2}.
\tag{27}
\]
If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
=1-\frac1{p^2}.
\tag{28}
\]
All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).

Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
\[
\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
\]
Thus (26) equals precisely
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
\]
This proves every assertion of P1.

No numerical checks or external sources were used.
=========== P2 statement
# P2: Variance reduction and disposal of initial moduli

Let f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and c=ζ(2)^(−1), where ζ is the Riemann zeta function. For real x≥2 and integers 1≤m≤x define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m). For real 1≤z≤y with Z=f(z)≤Y=f(y)≤x, define V_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}E(x;f(k),l)², T_f(z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)², and S_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{1≤h≤x/f(k)}C_x(hf(k)); all sums over k and h are over positive integers. For every ε>0 there is C(f,ε)>0 such that, uniformly throughout these ranges, |V_f(x;z,y)−[cx(Y−Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)−x²T_f(z,y)]|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/2+ε)+xY^(1−1/d)]. In addition, uniformly for x≥2 and real z≥1 with f(z)≤x, 0≤V_f(x,z)≤C(f,ε)x^(1+ε)f(z)^(2−1/d).
=========== P2 proof
# Proof of P2

All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
parameter, as indicated.

**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put

\[
\alpha=1-\frac1d.
\]

There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
that, for every real \(t\ge1\),

\[
 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure

\[
 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
\]

These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).

For the interval in the proposition, write

\[
 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
\]

Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
one each. Consequently,

\[
 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant

\[
 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
\]

satisfies

\[
 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
\]

Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).

We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
a finite \(D_\eta\) such that

\[
 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
\]

Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).

**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
define

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
\]

where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
\]

This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
has absolute value at most

\[
 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
 \le2\sqrt x.
\]

Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),

\[
 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
\]

Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put

\[
 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
\]

By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
in P1 therefore gives the exact identity

\[
 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
                                                                    \tag{7}
\]

Set

\[
 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
\]

The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
\]

There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,

\[
 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
\]

Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if

\[
 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
\]

then (8) proves the uniform estimate

\[
 |M(x;q)|
 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
\]

Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
\]

**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
residue class gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
\]

Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
including for nonintegral \(x\).

Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
\(M(x;q)\), gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
\]

Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly

\[
 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
\]

We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives

\[
 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
 \le3\sqrt x W
 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
\]

The endpoint error in (13) satisfies

\[
 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
\]

For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
\(f(k)\le x\) give

\[
 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
\]

There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields

\[
 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
\]

For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),

\[
 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
\]

The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives

\[
 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
\]

Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
most

\[
 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
\]

Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves

\[
 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
\]

This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).

**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
notation typeset in LaTeX, is:

> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
> number \(\varepsilon\),
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
> \begin{cases}
> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
> \end{cases}
> \]

The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are

> \[
> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
> \]
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
> \]

Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).

We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),

\[
 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
\]

Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that

\[
 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
\]

Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is

\[
 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
\]

The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are

\[
 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
 2-\frac22=1.
\]

It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
such that

\[
 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
\]

The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
image of the relevant supplied PDF page.

**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
weight bound

\[
 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
\]

Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
we obtain

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
\]

To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
\]

Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.

**Source and verification notes.** R. C. Vaughan, *A variance for k-free
numbers in arithmetic progressions* (2005), *Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society* (3) **91**, 573--597,
[DOI:10.1112/S0024611505015352](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352),
was consulted as a bibliographical pointer to the 1998 lemma. The estimate
used in the proof is the verbatim lemma quoted above from the supplied
1998 paper. A bibliographical web search returned post-2010 sources;
reading stopped when their dates were identified, and their content was
excluded from the argument.

A Python sanity check tested (9) and the exact identity (12) for all
integers \(1\le q\le\lfloor x\rfloor\), with
\(x\in\{2,3.25,10,31.75,100,200.5\}\), comprising 346 pairs \((x,q)\).
It used direct squarefree counts and the density formula of P1. Identity
(12) agreed within floating-point tolerance, and every test satisfied
(9). These computations serve only as checks; the proofs of (9) and
(12) are the finite identities and inequalities above.

38	converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
39	\[
40	x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
41	\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
42	\tag{4}
43	\]
44	Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
45	\[
46	|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
47	\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
48	\qquad x\geq1.
49	\tag{5}
50	\]
51	Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).
52	
53	We will use the elementary Euler identity
54	\[
55	c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
56	\tag{6}
57	\]
58	To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).
59	
60	For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
61	\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
62	\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
63	\[
64	\begin{cases}
65	1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
66	1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
67	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
68	1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
69	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
70	\end{cases}
71	\tag{7}
72	\]
73	This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).
74	
75	If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
76	\[
77	g(q,l)=\frac cq
78	\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
79	\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
80	\tag{8}
81	\]
82	Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
83	\[
84	0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
85	\tag{9}
86	\]

88	## The finite second-moment identity
89	
90	Let
91	\[
92	L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
93	\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
94	\]
95	The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
96	\[
97	L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
98	L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
99	L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
100	\tag{10}
101	\]
102	These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.
103	
104	For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
105	\[
106	b_{p,t}(l)=
107	\begin{cases}
108	1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
109	0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
110	1,&\text{otherwise}.
111	\end{cases}
112	\]
113	Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
114	\[
115	qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
116	(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
117	\tag{11}
118	\]
119	For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
120	\[
121	\begin{aligned}
122	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
123	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
124	\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
125	&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
126	&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
127	\end{aligned}
128	\tag{12}
129	\]
130	For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
131	\[
132	\begin{aligned}
133	(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
134	\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
135	&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
136	&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
137	&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
138	\end{aligned}
139	\tag{13}
140	\]
141	The last equality uses
142	\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).
143	
144	The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
145	\[
146	\begin{aligned}
147	q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
148	&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
149	&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
150	\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
151	&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
152	=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
153	\end{aligned}
154	\tag{14}
155	\]
156	
157	## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates
158	
159	The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
160	\[
161	r=ab^2,
162	\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
163	\tag{15}
164	\]
165	For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
166	\[
167	A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
168	\]
169	The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
170	\[
171	L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
172	L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
173	\]
174	Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
175	\[
176	0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
177	\tag{16}
178	\]
179	Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
180	\[
181	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
182	\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
183	\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
184	\leq3c^2<\infty,
185	\tag{17}
186	\]
187	where the two series are bounded by
188	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
189	\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.
190	
191	We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
192	\[
193	1+L(p)+L(p^2)
194	=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
195	\]
196	Consequently (6) implies
197	\[
198	\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
199	=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
200	=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
201	\tag{18}
202	\]
203	
204	For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
205	\[
206	\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
207	\tag{19}
208	\]
209	For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
210	\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
211	For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
212	For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
213	\[
214	\begin{aligned}
215	\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
216	&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
217	\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
218	&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
219	&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
220	\end{aligned}
221	\tag{20}
222	\]
223	For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
224	\[
225	\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
226	\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
227	\tag{21}
228	\]
229	
230	Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
231	\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
232	\[
233	\begin{aligned}
234	\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
235	&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
236	\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
237	&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
238	\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
239	\end{aligned}
240	\tag{22}
241	\]
242	For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
243	\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).
244	
245	For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.
246	
247	## The Ramanujan series
248	
249	There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
250	\[
251	|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
252	\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
253	\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
254	\tag{23}
255	\]
256	This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).
257	
258	For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
259	\[
260	\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
261	\]
262	Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
263	\[
264	c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
265	\tag{24}
266	\]
267	
268	The finite geometric sum satisfies
269	\[
270	\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
271	\]
272	Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
273	\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
274	Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
275	\[
276	c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
277	-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
278	\]
279	Adding these two exact identities yields
280	\[
281	c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
282	\tag{25}
283	\]
284	By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
285	\[
286	\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
287	=c^2\prod_p
288	\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
289	\tag{26}
290	\]
291	Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
292	\[
293	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
294	=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
295	=1-\frac2{p^2}.
296	\tag{27}
297	\]
298	If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
299	\[
300	(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
301	=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
302	=1-\frac1{p^2}.
303	\tag{28}
304	\]
305	All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
306	\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
307	\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).
308	
309	Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
310	\[
311	\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
312	\]
313	Thus (26) equals precisely
314	\[
315	\boxed{\displaystyle
316	\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
317	\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
318	\]
319	This proves every assertion of P1.
320	
321	No numerical checks or external sources were used.

323	# P2: Variance reduction and disposal of initial moduli
324	
325	Let f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and c=ζ(2)^(−1), where ζ is the Riemann zeta function. For real x≥2 and integers 1≤m≤x define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m). For real 1≤z≤y with Z=f(z)≤Y=f(y)≤x, define V_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}E(x;f(k),l)², T_f(z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)², and S_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{1≤h≤x/f(k)}C_x(hf(k)); all sums over k and h are over positive integers. For every ε>0 there is C(f,ε)>0 such that, uniformly throughout these ranges, |V_f(x;z,y)−[cx(Y−Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)−x²T_f(z,y)]|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/2+ε)+xY^(1−1/d)]. In addition, uniformly for x≥2 and real z≥1 with f(z)≤x, 0≤V_f(x,z)≤C(f,ε)x^(1+ε)f(z)^(2−1/d).
326	=========== P2 proof
327	# Proof of P2
328	
329	All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
330	the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
331	supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
332	density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
333	introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
334	parameter, as indicated.
335	
336	**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put
337	
338	\[
339	\alpha=1-\frac1d.
340	\]
341	
342	There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
343	that, for every real \(t\ge1\),
344	
345	\[
346	 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
347	 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
348	\]
349	
350	For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure
351	
352	\[
353	 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
354	\]
355	
356	These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
357	\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
358	infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
359	of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).
360	
361	For the interval in the proposition, write
362	
363	\[
364	 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
365	 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
366	\]
367	
368	Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
369	\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
370	\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
371	\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
372	absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
373	integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
374	one each. Consequently,
375	
376	\[
377	 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
378	 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
379	 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
380	\]
381	
382	For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
383	\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
384	in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant
385	
386	\[
387	 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
388	\]
389	
390	satisfies
391	
392	\[
393	 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
394	 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
395	\]
396	
397	Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).
398	
399	We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
400	denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
401	a finite \(D_\eta\) such that
402	
403	\[
404	 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
405	\]
406	
407	Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
408	\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
409	\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).
410	
411	**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
412	define
413	
414	\[
415	 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
416	 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
417	\]
418	
419	where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
420	converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
421	\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives
422	
423	\[
424	 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
425	              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
426	\]
427	
428	This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
429	has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
430	\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
431	has absolute value at most
432	
433	\[
434	 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
435	 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
436	 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
437	 \le2\sqrt x.
438	\]
439	
440	Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),
441	
442	\[
443	 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
444	\]
445	
446	Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put
447	
448	\[
449	 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
450	 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
451	 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
452	\]
453	
454	By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
455	\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
456	occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
457	in P1 therefore gives the exact identity
458	
459	\[
460	 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
461	 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
462	       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
463	                                                                    \tag{7}
464	\]
465	
466	Set
467	
468	\[
469	 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
470	\]
471	
472	The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
473	error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
474	value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,
475	
476	\[
477	 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
478	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
479	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
480	\]
481	
482	There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
483	\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,
484	
485	\[
486	 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
487	 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
488	\]
489	
490	Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
491	the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
492	Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if
493	
494	\[
495	 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
496	\]
497	
498	then (8) proves the uniform estimate
499	
500	\[
501	 |M(x;q)|
502	 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
503	 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
504	\]
505	
506	Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
507	\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives
508	
509	\[
510	 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
511	\]
512	
513	**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
514	\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
515	residue class gives
516	
517	\[
518	 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
519	 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
520	     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
521	\]
522	
523	Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
524	with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
525	one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
526	number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
527	their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
528	including for nonintegral \(x\).
529	
530	Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
531	\(M(x;q)\), gives
532	
533	\[
534	 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
535	 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
536	     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
537	     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
538	\]
539	
540	Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
541	and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
542	approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
543	Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly
544	
545	\[
546	 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
547	      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
548	      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
549	\]
550	
551	We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
552	over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
553	After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives
554	
555	\[
556	 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
557	 \le3\sqrt x W
558	 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
559	 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
560	\]
561	
562	The endpoint error in (13) satisfies
563	
564	\[
565	 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
566	\]
567	
568	For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
569	\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
570	\(f(k)\le x\) give
571	
572	\[
573	 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
574	 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
575	 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
576	\]
577	
578	There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
579	the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields
580	
581	\[
582	 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
583	 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
584	\]
585	
586	For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
587	follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
588	\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),
589	
590	\[
591	 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
592	 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
593	\]
594	
595	The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives
596	
597	\[
598	 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
599	 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
600	\]
601	
602	Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
603	before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
604	\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
605	most
606	
607	\[
608	 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
609	 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
610	\]
611	
612	Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves
613	
614	\[
615	 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
616	  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
617	 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
618	       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
619	\]
620	
621	This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).

623	**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
624	We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
625	Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
626	*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
627	739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
628	The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
629	6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
630	notation typeset in LaTeX, is:
631	
632	> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
633	> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
634	> number \(\varepsilon\),
635	> \[
636	> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
637	> \begin{cases}
638	> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
639	> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
640	> \end{cases}
641	> \]
642	
643	The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are
644	
645	> \[
646	> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
647	> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
648	> \]
649	> \[
650	> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
651	>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
652	> \]
653	
654	Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
655	integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
656	index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).
657	
658	We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
659	source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
660	apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
661	parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
662	These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
663	a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
664	term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),
665	
666	\[
667	 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
668	 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
669	       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
670	\]
671	
672	Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that
673	
674	\[
675	 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
676	 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
677	\]
678	
679	Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is
680	
681	\[
682	 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
683	\]
684	
685	The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
686	coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
687	parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are
688	
689	\[
690	 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
691	 2-\frac22=1.
692	\]
693	
694	It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
695	such that
696	
697	\[
698	 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
699	       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
700	\]
701	
702	The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
703	image of the relevant supplied PDF page.
704	
705	**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
706	\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
707	For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
708	weight bound
709	
710	\[
711	 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
712	\]
713	
714	Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
715	\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
716	are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
717	\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
718	(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
719	corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
720	terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
721	we obtain
722	
723	\[
724	 0\le V_f(x,z)
725	 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
726	       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
727	 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
728	\]
729	
730	To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
731	positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
732	the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
733	the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
734	quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield
735	
736	\[
737	 0\le V_f(x,z)
738	 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
739	       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
740	 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
741	       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
742	\]
743	
744	Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
745	proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.

764	=========== P3 statement
765	# P3: Uniform correlation estimate for squarefree numbers
766	
767	For real x≥2 and every integer 1≤m≤x, define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m) and 𝔖(m)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|m}(p²−1)/(p²−2), with products over primes. For every ε>0 there is C(ε)>0 such that |C_x(m)−(x−m)𝔖(m)|≤C(ε)x^(4/5+ε), uniformly for all such x and m. A permitted circle-method cutoff is Q=x^(2/5), for x sufficiently large that Q≤x^(1/2)/2; the major arcs are the subsets of R/Z with |α−a/q|≤Q/(qx), 1≤q≤Q and gcd(a,q)=1. The bound is uniform even when x−m is bounded.
768	=========== P3 proof
769	# Proof of P3
770	
771	We prove the stronger bound
772	\[
773	\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
774	\tag{1}
775	\]
776	with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
777	The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
778	No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
779	dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.
780	
781	## An explicit divisor bound
782	
783	Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
784	\(n\). Define the absolute constant
785	\[
786	D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
787	\]
788	where the product is over primes. We will use
789	\[
790	\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
791	\tag{2}
792	\]
793	Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
794	\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
795	then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
796	\[
797	(a+1)p^{-a/10}
798	\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
799	=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
800	\]
801	Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
802	(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
803	all at least one.
804	
805	We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
806	integers \(H\):
807	\[
808	\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
809	\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
810	\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
811	\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
812	\tag{3}
813	\]
814	The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
815	integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
816	Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).
817	
818	## Truncating the square-divisor identities
819	
820	Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
821	\[
822	L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
823	\]
824	In particular,
825	\[
826	\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
827	\tag{4}
828	\]
829	For positive integers \(k\), define
830	\[
831	T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
832	R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
833	\]
834	All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
835	\[
836	\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
837	\tag{5}
838	\]
839	follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
840	least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
841	Also
842	\[
843	|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
844	|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
845	\tag{6}
846	\]
847	
848	For either of the two sets
849	\[
850	I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
851	I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
852	\]
853	there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
854	For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
855	\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
856	\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
857	for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
858	\[
859	\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
860	\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
861	\le\frac{x}{H}.
862	\tag{7}
863	\]
864	This estimate also holds when either set is empty.
865	
866	The exact product identity
867	\[
868	\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
869	=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
870	\]
871	and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
872	most
873	\[
874	|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
875	\]
876	where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
877	\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
878	each of its two terms, yields
879	\[
880	\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
881	\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
882	\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
883	\tag{8}
884	\]
885	In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).
886	
887	## Counting the truncated congruences
888	
889	For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
890	\[
891	n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
892	\]
893	are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
894	both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
895	the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
896	\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
897	\[
898	a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
899	\]
900	Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
901	\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
902	\[
903	h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
904	\]
905	For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
906	number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
907	\[
908	\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
909	-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
910	=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
911	\tag{9}
912	\]
913	This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).
914	
915	Define
916	\[
917	A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
918	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
919	\]
920	Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
921	\[
922	\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
923	\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
924	\tag{10}
925	\]
926	Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
927	at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
928	most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.
929	
930	## The infinite main term and its uniform tail
931	
932	Consider
933	\[
934	A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
935	\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
936	\]
937	This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
938	with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
939	absolute sum by
940	\[
941	\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
942	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
943	   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
944	   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
945	\le8.
946	\tag{11}
947	\]
948	
949	We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
950	\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
951	\[
952	\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
953	\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
954	  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
955	  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
956	\tag{12}
957	\]
958	For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
959	\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
960	and their total is at most
961	\[
962	\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
963	\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
964	\]
965	For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
966	\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
967	\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
968	\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
969	bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
970	\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
971	bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
972	\[
973	|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
974	=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
975	\tag{13}
976	\]
977	All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
978	\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).
979	
980	Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
981	one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
982	finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
983	exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
984	For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
985	follows:
986	
987	| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
988	| --- | --- | --- |
989	| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
990	| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
991	| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
992	| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |
993	
994	It follows that
995	\[
996	\begin{aligned}
997	A(m)
998	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
999	                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
1000	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
1001	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
1002	  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
1003	&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
1004	  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
1005	=\mathfrak S(m).
1006	\end{aligned}
1007	\tag{14}
1008	\]
1009	The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
1010	because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.
1011	
1012	## Combining the bounds
1013	
1014	Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
1015	\[
1016	\begin{aligned}
1017	L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
1018	&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
1019	&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
1020	&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
1021	\end{aligned}
1022	\tag{15}
1023	\]
1024	For \(x\ge1\),
1025	\[
1026	\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
1027	\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
1028	=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
1029	\]
1030	Thus (15) is at most
1031	\[
1032	32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
1033	\tag{16}
1034	\]
1035	Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
1036	\[
1037	\begin{aligned}
1038	\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
1039	&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
1040	&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
1041	\end{aligned}
1042	\]
1043	This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
1044	\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
1045	\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
1046	\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
1047	uniformity. \(\square\)
