=========== P1 statement
# P1: Local densities and summable spectral coefficients

Let μ be the Möbius function, φ Euler's totient, ζ the Riemann zeta function, and c=ζ(2)^(−1). All products below are over primes. For every integer q≥1 and integer l, the density g(q,l) from problem.md equals q^(−1)Σ_{m≥1, gcd(m²,q)|l} μ(m)gcd(m²,q)/m². Equivalently, it is zero if some p² divides both q and l; otherwise it equals (c/q)∏_{p|q}(1−p^(−2))^(−1)∏_{p||q, p|l}(1−p^(−1)). In particular 0≤g(q,l)≤1/q. Define the multiplicative function G by G(1)=1, G(p)=G(p²)=−1/(p²−1), and G(p^a)=0 for a≥3. Put γ(r)=cG(r), λ(r)=φ(r)γ(r)², and c_r(n)=Σ_{1≤a≤r, gcd(a,r)=1} exp(2πian/r). Then qΣ_{l=1}^q g(q,l)²=Σ_{r|q}λ(r), Σ_{r≥1}λ(r)=c, and, for every integer n≥1, the absolutely convergent series Σ_{r≥1}γ(r)²c_r(n) equals 𝔖(n)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|n}(p²−1)/(p²−2). There is an absolute constant C such that, uniformly for real R≥2, Σ_{r>R}λ(r)≤CR^(−1/2)(log(2R))² and Σ_{r≤R}rλ(r)≤CR^(1/2)(log(2R))².
=========== P1 proof
# Proof of P1

Write \(e(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\), and take logarithms to base \(e\). All sums over integers below are over positive integers unless another range is specified. We prove the assertions directly; no external literature or dependency proposition is used.

## Existence and evaluation of the density

For every positive integer \(n\), prime factorization gives
\[
\sum_{m^2\mid n}\mu(m)
=\prod_{p^2\mid n}(1-1)=\mu^2(n),
\tag{1}
\]
where an empty product equals one. Fix \(q\geq1\) and \(l\in\mathbb Z\). For \(x\geq1\), put \(M=\lfloor\sqrt{x}\rfloor\) and \(d_m=(m^2,q)\). The simultaneous congruences
\[
n\equiv l\pmod q,\qquad n\equiv0\pmod{m^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(d_m\mid l\). Indeed, writing \(n=m^2k\) reduces them to a linear congruence in \(k\); division by \(d_m\) leaves a coefficient coprime to \(q/d_m\). When soluble, the solutions form one residue class modulo \(qm^2/d_m\). The number of its members in \([1,x]\) differs from \(xd_m/(qm^2)\) by at most one. Consequently (1) gives
\[
Q(x;q,l)=\frac{x}{q}
\sum_{\substack{m\leq M\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}+E_1,
\qquad |E_1|\leq M.
\tag{2}
\]
Here each counting error has absolute value at most one, and there are at most \(M\) terms, so their sum has absolute value at most \(M\).

The series
\[
D(q,l)=\frac1q\sum_{\substack{m\geq1\\d_m\mid l}}
\frac{\mu(m)d_m}{m^2}
\tag{3}
\]
converges absolutely: each summand has absolute value at most \(m^{-2}\), since \(d_m\leq q\). The infinite omitted tail in (2), after multiplication by \(x\), has absolute value at most
\[
x\sum_{m>M}\frac1{m^2}
\leq x\int_M^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=\frac{x}{M}.
\tag{4}
\]
Since \(\sqrt{x}/2\leq M\leq\sqrt{x}\), equations (2)--(4) prove the explicit estimate
\[
|Q(x;q,l)-xD(q,l)|
\leq M+\frac{x}{M}\leq3\sqrt{x},
\qquad x\geq1.
\tag{5}
\]
Dividing by \(x\) and letting \(x\) tend to infinity proves that the density from `problem.md` exists and equals (3).

We will use the elementary Euler identity
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1}=\prod_p(1-p^{-2}).
\tag{6}
\]
To justify it here, expanding \(\prod_{p\leq z}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\) gives the sum of \(m^{-2}\) over integers all of whose prime factors are at most \(z\). These sums increase to \(\sum_{m\geq1}m^{-2}=\zeta(2)\), because every integer has finitely many prime factors. Taking reciprocals gives (6).

For a prime \(p\), let \(t=v_p(q)\). The summand in (3) vanishes unless \(m\) is squarefree. The choice to include \(p\) in such an \(m\) contributes
\(-p^{\min(2,t)-2}\), and is allowed precisely when
\(p^{\min(2,t)}\mid l\). Thus the local factor in \(qg(q,l)\) is
\[
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-2},&t=0,\\
1,&t=1,\ p\nmid l,\\
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
1,&t\geq2,\ p^2\nmid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l.
\end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
This Euler expansion is justified by the absolute convergence of (3); equivalently, expand over finitely many primes and pass to the absolutely convergent series. The divisibility conditions in (7) also apply to \(l=0\).

If some \(p^2\) divides both \(q\) and \(l\), (7) gives \(g(q,l)=0\). In every other case, combining (6) and (7) gives exactly
\[
g(q,l)=\frac cq
\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1}
\prod_{\substack{p\parallel q\\p\mid l}}(1-p^{-1}).
\tag{8}
\]
Every local factor in (7) lies in \([0,1]\). Their product therefore lies in \([0,1]\), proving
\[
0\leq g(q,l)\leq\frac1q.
\tag{9}
\]

## The finite second-moment identity

Let
\[
L(r)=\varphi(r)G(r)^2,
\qquad \lambda(r)=c^2L(r).
\]
The function \(L\) is multiplicative. Its prime-power values are
\[
L(p)=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{p(p-1)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
L(p^j)=0\quad(j\geq3).
\tag{10}
\]
These formulas follow from counting the \(p^j-p^{j-1}\) residues coprime to \(p^j\); multiplicativity of \(\varphi\) follows from the Chinese remainder theorem.

For \(t\geq1\), define a function on residues modulo \(p^t\) by
\[
b_{p,t}(l)=
\begin{cases}
1-p^{-1},&t=1,\ p\mid l,\\
0,&t\geq2,\ p^2\mid l,\\
1,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Equations (7)--(8), including their zero cases, give
\[
qg(q,l)=c\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
(1-p^{-2})^{-1}b_{p,t}(l).
\tag{11}
\]
For \(t=1\), there are \(p-1\) residues with \(b_{p,1}=1\) and one with \(b_{p,1}=1-p^{-1}\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1p\sum_{l\bmod p}b_{p,1}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-2}
\left(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^3}\right)\\
&=\frac{p^4-2p^2+p}{(p^2-1)^2}\\
&=1+\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2}=1+L(p).
\end{aligned}
\tag{12}
\]
For \(t\geq2\), precisely \(p^{t-2}\) of the \(p^t\) residues have \(b_{p,t}=0\), and the other \(p^t-p^{t-2}\) have value one. Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
(1-p^{-2})^{-2}\frac1{p^t}
\sum_{l\bmod p^t}b_{p,t}(l)^2
&=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}\\
&=1+\frac1{p^2-1}\\
&=1+L(p)+L(p^2).
\end{aligned}
\tag{13}
\]
The last equality uses
\((p-1)+p(p-1)=p^2-1\).

The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the \(q\) residues modulo \(q\) with the Cartesian product of the residue sets modulo its prime-power factors. Averaging the square of (11) consequently factors into the local averages (12)--(13). With empty products understood when \(q=1\), this yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
q\sum_{l=1}^qg(q,l)^2
&=\frac1q\sum_{l=1}^q(qg(q,l))^2\\
&=c^2\prod_{p^t\parallel q}
\left(1+\sum_{j=1}^tL(p^j)\right)\\
&=c^2\sum_{r\mid q}L(r)
=\sum_{r\mid q}\lambda(r).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]

## Absolute summability and explicit tail estimates

The support of \(L\) consists of integers with no prime exponent exceeding two. Every such integer has a unique representation
\[
r=ab^2,
\qquad a,b\text{ squarefree},\quad(a,b)=1.
\tag{15}
\]
For every prime \(p\geq2\), set
\[
A_p=\frac{p^3}{(p-1)(p+1)^2}.
\]
The denominator minus the numerator equals \(p^2-p-1\), which is at least one for \(p\geq2\). Thus \(0<A_p\leq1\), and (10) becomes
\[
L(p)=\frac{A_p}{p^3},\qquad
L(p^2)=\frac{A_p}{p^2}.
\]
Multiplying these inequalities over the prime factors in (15) proves
\[
0\leq\lambda(ab^2)\leq\frac{c^2}{a^3b^2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Dropping the restrictions on \(a,b\) only increases these nonnegative sums. In particular
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
\leq c^2\left(\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-3}\right)
\left(\sum_{b\geq1}b^{-2}\right)
\leq3c^2<\infty,
\tag{17}
\]
where the two series are bounded by
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-3}dt=3/2\) and
\(1+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}dt=2\), respectively.

We can now evaluate the sum by its absolutely convergent Euler product. Equation (10) gives
\[
1+L(p)+L(p^2)
=1+\frac1{p^2-1}=(1-p^{-2})^{-1}.
\]
Consequently (6) implies
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)
=c^2\prod_p(1+L(p)+L(p^2))
=c^2\zeta(2)=c.
\tag{18}
\]

For every real \(T>0\), we have the explicit bound
\[
\sum_{b>T}\frac1{b^2}\leq\frac2T.
\tag{19}
\]
For \(T\geq1\), putting \(N=\lfloor T\rfloor\geq T/2\) bounds this infinite tail by
\(\int_N^\infty t^{-2}dt=1/N\leq2/T\).
For \(0<T<1\), the sum is at most \(2\), which is at most \(2/T\).
For any \(R>0\), (16) and then (19), with \(T=\sqrt{R/a}\), give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{a\geq1}\frac1{a^3}
\sum_{b>\sqrt{R/a}}\frac1{b^2}\\
&\leq2c^2R^{-1/2}\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}\\
&\leq\frac{10}{3}R^{-1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{20}
\]
For each \(a\), the inner infinite sum before summation over \(a\) is at most \(2\sqrt{a/R}\). Its contribution after multiplication by \(c^2a^{-3}\) is at most \(2c^2R^{-1/2}a^{-5/2}\). The final bound uses \(c\leq1\) and
\[
\sum_{a\geq1}a^{-5/2}
\leq1+\int_1^\infty t^{-5/2}dt=\frac53.
\tag{21}
\]

Multiplication of (16) by \(ab^2\) gives
\(ab^2\lambda(ab^2)\leq c^2a^{-2}\). Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r)
&\leq c^2\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}\frac1{a^2}
\sum_{1\leq b\leq\sqrt{R/a}}1\\
&\leq c^2R^{1/2}\sum_{1\leq a\leq R}a^{-5/2}
\leq\frac53R^{1/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{22}
\]
For each \(a\leq R\), the inner sum has
\(\lfloor\sqrt{R/a}\rfloor\leq\sqrt{R/a}\) terms, each contributing at most \(c^2a^{-2}\). Its total is at most \(c^2R^{1/2}a^{-5/2}\). Summing over the \(\lfloor R\rfloor\) possible values of \(a\), and applying (21), gives the last inequality in (22).

For \(R\geq2\), \(\log(2R)\geq\log4>1\). Therefore (20) and (22) imply both bounds requested in the statement, with the same absolute constant \(C=10/3\). They also prove the stronger versions without logarithmic factors.

## The Ramanujan series

There are \(\varphi(r)\) terms in the defining sum for \(c_r(n)\), each of absolute value one. Hence, for every integer \(n\),
\[
|c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
\sum_{r\geq1}|\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)|
\leq\sum_{r\geq1}\lambda(r)=c.
\tag{23}
\]
This proves absolute convergence, with a bound uniform in \(n\).

For completeness, the multiplicativity needed to evaluate the series follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem. If \((s,t)=1\), choose integers \(u,v\) with \(tu\equiv1\pmod s\) and \(sv\equiv1\pmod t\). A unit residue \(a\pmod{st}\) corresponding to unit residues \(b\pmod s\), \(d\pmod t\) satisfies
\[
\frac{a}{st}\equiv\frac{bu}{s}+\frac{dv}{t}\pmod1.
\]
Summing the resulting exponential identity over \(b,d\), and using the permutations of unit residues induced by multiplication by \(u,v\), gives
\[
c_{st}(n)=c_s(n)c_t(n).
\tag{24}
\]

The finite geometric sum satisfies
\[
\sum_{a=1}^k e(an/k)=k\,\boldsymbol1_{k\mid n}.
\]
Subtracting the term for the zero residue modulo \(p\) gives
\(c_p(n)=p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}-1\).
Subtracting the sum over residues divisible by \(p\) from the full sum modulo \(p^2\) gives
\[
c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}
-p\boldsymbol1_{p\mid n}.
\]
Adding these two exact identities yields
\[
c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\boldsymbol1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
\tag{25}
\]
By (23)--(24), the absolutely convergent series has the Euler expansion
\[
\sum_{r\geq1}\gamma(r)^2c_r(n)
=c^2\prod_p
\left(1+\frac{c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)}{(p^2-1)^2}\right).
\tag{26}
\]
Using (6), absorb the factor \((1-p^{-2})^2\) of \(c^2\) into each local factor. If \(p^2\nmid n\), (25) gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1-\frac1{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{(p^2-1)^2-1}{p^4}
=1-\frac2{p^2}.
\tag{27}
\]
If \(p^2\mid n\), it gives
\[
(1-p^{-2})^2\left(1+\frac{p^2-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2}
=1-\frac1{p^2}.
\tag{28}
\]
All these product operations are legitimate: (26) is justified by absolute convergence, and (6) converges. The product \(\prod_p(1-2/p^2)\) converges to a positive number as well. Indeed, for \(0\leq u\leq1/2\),
\(-\log(1-u)=\int_0^u(1-t)^{-1}dt\leq2u\), so
\(\sum_p|\log(1-2/p^2)|\leq4\sum_p p^{-2}<\infty\).

Finally, when \(n\geq1\), only finitely many primes satisfy \(p^2\mid n\). Replacing the factors (27) by (28) for those primes multiplies the baseline product by
\[
\frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}=\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.
\]
Thus (26) equals precisely
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\mathfrak S(n)=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
\prod_{p^2\mid n}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}.}
\]
This proves every assertion of P1.

No numerical checks or external sources were used.
=========== P2 statement
# P2: Variance reduction and disposal of initial moduli

Let f be as in problem.md, d=deg f, and c=ζ(2)^(−1), where ζ is the Riemann zeta function. For real x≥2 and integers 1≤m≤x define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m). For real 1≤z≤y with Z=f(z)≤Y=f(y)≤x, define V_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}E(x;f(k),l)², T_f(z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)², and S_f(x;z,y)=Σ_{z<k≤y}f'(k)Σ_{1≤h≤x/f(k)}C_x(hf(k)); all sums over k and h are over positive integers. For every ε>0 there is C(f,ε)>0 such that, uniformly throughout these ranges, |V_f(x;z,y)−[cx(Y−Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)−x²T_f(z,y)]|≤C(f,ε)[x^(3/2+ε)+xY^(1−1/d)]. In addition, uniformly for x≥2 and real z≥1 with f(z)≤x, 0≤V_f(x,z)≤C(f,ε)x^(1+ε)f(z)^(2−1/d).
=========== P2 proof
# Proof of P2

All counting variables are positive integers, unless stated otherwise. We use
the definitions of \(Q,g,E,V_f\) in `problem.md` and assume P1 exactly as
supplied. In particular, \(g(q,l)\) is periodic in \(l\), is real, and is the
density of squarefree integers in the indicated residue class. Constants
introduced below depend only on \(f\), or on the displayed positive error
parameter, as indicated.

**1. Polynomial weights and endpoints.** Put

\[
\alpha=1-\frac1d.
\]

There are constants \(0<A\le1\) and \(B\ge1\), depending only on \(f\), such
that, for every real \(t\ge1\),

\[
 At^d\le f(t)\le Bt^d,\qquad
 1\le f'(t)\le Bt^{d-1}.                                      \tag{1}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), enlarge \(B\) to ensure

\[
 |f''(t)|\le Bt^{d-2}\quad(t\ge1).                            \tag{2}
\]

These constants exist because the leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive,
\(f(t)/t^d\) is positive and continuous on \([1,\infty)\), and its limit at
infinity is positive. The upper bounds follow by bounding each coefficient
of the relevant polynomial. For \(d=1\), \(f''=0\).

For the interval in the proposition, write

\[
 W=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k),\qquad
 N=\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor.
\]

Thus this sum has exactly \(N\le y\) terms. Let \(n=\lfloor z\rfloor\) and
\(m=\lfloor y\rfloor\). For each of its \(N\) terms, the error on replacing
\(f'(k)\) by its integral over \([k-1,k]\) has absolute value at most
\(\int_{k-1}^k|f''(t)|\,dt\). After summing these \(N\) errors, their total
absolute value is at most \(\int_n^m|f''(t)|\,dt\). The two endpoint
integrals needed to replace \([n,m]\) by \([z,y]\) have lengths less than
one each. Consequently,

\[
 \left|W-\int_z^y f'(t)\,dt\right|
 \le 2\sup_{1\le t\le y}f'(t)+\int_1^y|f''(t)|\,dt
 \le 3B y^{d-1}.                                             \tag{3}
\]

For \(d\ge2\), the integral in this inequality is at most
\(B(y^{d-1}-1)/(d-1)\le By^{d-1}\). For \(d=1\), it is zero, so (3) holds
in that case as well. Since \(Y=f(y)\ge Ay^d\), the constant

\[
 K=3BA^{-\alpha}
\]

satisfies

\[
 |W-(Y-Z)|\le K Y^\alpha,\qquad
 0\le W\le(1+K)Y.                                           \tag{4}
\]

Here we used \(Y\ge2\) and \(Y^\alpha\le Y\).

We shall also use the following elementary divisor bound. If \(\tau(q)\)
denotes the number of divisors of \(q\), then for every \(\eta>0\) there is
a finite \(D_\eta\) such that

\[
 \tau(q)\le D_\eta q^\eta\quad(q\ge1).                       \tag{5}
\]

Indeed, for primes \(p\ge2^{1/\eta}\) and integers \(e\ge0\),
\(e+1\le2^e\le p^{\eta e}\). For each of the finitely many smaller primes,
\(\sup_{e\ge0}(e+1)p^{-\eta e}\) is finite. Their product gives \(D_\eta\).

**2. An elementary mixed-moment estimate.** For a positive integer \(a\),
define

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{\substack{n\le x\\a\mid n}}\mu^2(n),\qquad
 D_a=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\mu(r)}{[a,r^2]},
\]

where brackets denote the least common multiple. The series for \(D_a\)
converges absolutely because \([a,r^2]\ge r^2\). The elementary identity
\(\mu^2(n)=\sum_{r^2\mid n}\mu(r)\) gives

\[
 N_a(x)=\sum_{r\le\sqrt x}\mu(r)
              \left\lfloor\frac{x}{[a,r^2]}\right\rfloor.
\]

This \(r\)-sum has \(\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor\) terms. Each floor replacement
has error of absolute value at most one; their total error is at most
\(\sqrt x\). The omitted part of the absolutely convergent main-term series
has absolute value at most

\[
 x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{[a,r^2]}
 \le x\sum_{r>\sqrt x}\frac1{r^2}
 \le\frac{x}{\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor}
 \le2\sqrt x.
\]

Thus, uniformly in \(a\ge1\) and real \(x\ge2\),

\[
 |N_a(x)-xD_a|\le3\sqrt x.                                  \tag{6}
\]

Fix a positive integer \(q\), and put

\[
 q_1=\prod_{p\parallel q}p,\qquad
 A_q=\prod_{p\mid q}(1-p^{-2})^{-1},\qquad
 H(q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)^2.
\]

By the absolutely convergent Euler product for \(\zeta(2)\),
\(cA_q\le1\). For squarefree \(n\), the zero-density exception in P1 never
occurs, since no prime square divides \(n\). Expanding the remaining factors
in P1 therefore gives the exact identity

\[
 \mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\frac{cA_q}{q}\mu^2(n)
       \sum_{\substack{a\mid q_1\\a\mid n}}\frac{\mu(a)}a.
                                                                    \tag{7}
\]

Set

\[
 B(q)=\frac{cA_q}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac{\mu(a)}aD_a.
\]

The divisor sum here has \(\tau(q_1)\le\tau(q)\) terms. Before summing, the
error contributed by a divisor \(a\), on using (6) in (7), has absolute
value at most \(3cA_q\sqrt x/(qa)\). After summing over these divisors,

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xB(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\sum_{a\mid q_1}\frac1a
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{8}
\]

There is no uniform-limit issue in identifying \(B(q)\). For this fixed
\(q\), periodicity gives a sum of exactly \(q\) residue classes,

\[
 \sum_{n\le t}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)
 =\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)Q(t;q,l).
\]

Divide by \(t\) and let \(t\to\infty\). By the definition of the densities,
the right side tends to \(H(q)\); by (8), the left side tends to \(B(q)\).
Hence \(B(q)=H(q)\). In particular, if

\[
 M(x;q)=\sum_{l=1}^q g(q,l)E(x;q,l),
\]

then (8) proves the uniform estimate

\[
 |M(x;q)|
 =\left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)g(q,n)-xH(q)\right|
 \le\frac{3\sqrt x}{q}\tau(q).                               \tag{9}
\]

Taking \(a=1\) in (6), the Euler product
\(D_1=\sum_{r\ge1}\mu(r)/r^2=c\) also gives

\[
 \left|\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right|\le3\sqrt x.           \tag{10}
\]

**3. Exact expansion and its accumulated errors.** For every integer
\(1\le q\le x\), counting ordered pairs of squarefree integers in the same
residue class gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q Q(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq).                         \tag{11}
\]

Indeed, pairs with equal coordinates contribute the first term. For a pair
with unequal coordinates, its positive difference is exactly \(hq\) for
one of the \(\lfloor x/q\rfloor\) possible positive integers \(h\). The
number of such pairs in increasing order is \(C_x(hq)\), and reversing
their order gives the factor two. These are exact finite identities,
including for nonintegral \(x\).

Since \(Q=E+xg\), expansion of the square, followed by the definition of
\(M(x;q)\), gives

\[
 \sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)
     +2\sum_{1\le h\le x/q}C_x(hq)
     -x^2H(q)-2xM(x;q).                                     \tag{12}
\]

Sum this identity over the \(N\) integers \(z<k\le y\), with \(q=f(k)\)
and weight \(f'(k)\). The hypotheses imply \(q\le Y\le x\). There is no
approximation in the correlation sum or in the term containing \(H(q)\).
Thus the difference asserted in the first part of P2 is exactly

\[
 R=\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W
      +cx\bigl(W-(Y-Z)\bigr)
      -2x\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k)).                     \tag{13}
\]

We bound each of these three errors. Before summing the diagonal error
over \(k\), its absolute value is at most \(3\sqrt x f'(k)\), by (10).
After summing its \(N\) terms, (4) gives

\[
 \left|\left(\sum_{n\le x}\mu^2(n)-cx\right)W\right|
 \le3\sqrt x W
 \le3(1+K)\sqrt x Y
 \le3(1+K)x^{3/2}.                                          \tag{14}
\]

The endpoint error in (13) satisfies

\[
 |cx(W-(Y-Z))|\le cKxY^\alpha.                              \tag{15}
\]

For the mixed error, fix the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\) and set
\(\eta=\varepsilon/2\). Before summing over \(k\), (1), (5), (9), and
\(f(k)\le x\) give

\[
 |f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le3D_\eta x^{1/2+\eta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}\frac{x^{1/2+\eta}}{k}.              \tag{16}
\]

There are \(N\le\lfloor y\rfloor\le A^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) terms. Summing
the displayed reciprocal bound, rather than its maximum, yields

\[
 \sum_{z<k\le y}|f'(k)M(x;f(k))|
 \le\frac{3D_\eta B}{A}x^{1/2+\eta}(1+\log y).              \tag{17}
\]

For completeness, \(\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor y\rfloor}1/k\le1+\log y\)
follows by bounding the terms with \(k\ge2\) by
\(\int_{k-1}^{k}dt/t\). From \(Ay^d\le x\),

\[
 1+\log y\le L\log(2x),\qquad
 L=1+\frac1d+\frac{\log(A^{-1})}{d}.
\]

The elementary maximum of \(u e^{-\eta u}\), for \(u\ge0\), gives

\[
 \log(2x)\le J_\eta x^\eta,\qquad
 J_\eta=\log2+\frac1{e\eta}\quad(x\ge2).
\]

Consequently, with \(M_{f,\varepsilon}=3D_\eta BLJ_\eta/A\), the error
before multiplication by \(2x\) in (13) is at most
\(M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1/2+2\eta}\). After that multiplication it is at
most

\[
 2x\left|\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)M(x;f(k))\right|
 \le2M_{f,\varepsilon}x^{3/2+\varepsilon}.                   \tag{18}
\]

Combining (13)--(18), and using \(x^{3/2}\le x^{3/2+\varepsilon}\), proves

\[
 \left|V_f(x;z,y)
  -\{cx(Y-Z)+2S_f(x;z,y)-x^2T_f(z,y)\}\right|
 \le\bigl(3(1+K)+2M_{f,\varepsilon}\bigr)x^{3/2+\varepsilon}
       +cKxY^{1-1/d}.                                      \tag{19}
\]

This also covers \(z=y\), and intervals containing no integer \(k\).

**4. The published full-variance bound, with its normalization checked.**
We use J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D.
Wooley, *On the exponential sum over k-free numbers* (1998),
*Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London A* **356**,
739--761, [DOI:10.1098/rsta.1998.0183](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183).
The reference is the supplied `papers/bgpvw-1998.pdf`, Lemma 2.2, on page
6 of that PDF. Its statement, quoted verbatim with its mathematical
notation typeset in LaTeX, is:

> **Lemma 2.2.** Suppose that \(Q\) and \(x\) are positive real numbers,
> and that \(k\) is an integer with \(k\ge2\). Then for each positive
> number \(\varepsilon\),
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)\ll
> \begin{cases}
> x^{2/k+\varepsilon}Q^{2-2/k},&\text{when }1\le Q\le x,\\
> Q^2\log(2Q),&\text{when }Q>x.
> \end{cases}
> \]

The source's defining equations (2.6) and (2.7), also quoted, are

> \[
> \sum_{\substack{1\le n\le x\\n\equiv a\pmod q}}\mu_k(n)
> =\frac{x}{\zeta(k)}g_k(q,(q,a))+E_k(x;q,a),                 \tag{2.6}
> \]
> \[
> \Upsilon_k(x,Q)=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q
>                          |E_k(x;q,a)|^2.                  \tag{2.7}
> \]

Here \(\mu_k\) is the source's characteristic function of the \(k\)-free
integers; its \(k\) is the power parameter, independent of our polynomial
index. In particular, \(\mu_2=\mu^2\).

We check the density normalization without assuming any formula for the
source's \(g_k\). Fix positive integers \(q,a\), with \(1\le a\le q\), and
apply the quoted lemma with power parameter \(k=2\), \(Q=q\), error
parameter \(1/2\), and real \(t\ge\max\{2,q\}\) in place of \(x\).
These are positive real \(Q,t\), an integer power parameter at least two,
a positive error parameter, and \(1\le Q\le t\), as required. Since each
term of (2.7) is nonnegative, the lemma implies, for a constant \(B_{1/2}\),

\[
 |E_2(t;q,a)|^2\le B_{1/2}t^{3/2}q,\qquad
 \frac{|E_2(t;q,a)|}{t}
       \le B_{1/2}^{1/2}q^{1/2}t^{-1/4}\longrightarrow0.
\]

Dividing (2.6) by \(t\) therefore shows that

\[
 c\,g_2(q,(q,a))
 =\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{Q(t;q,a)}t=g(q,a).
\]

Thus \(E_2(x;q,a)=E(x;q,a)\) exactly, and the source's sum (2.7) is

\[
 U(x,Q):=\sum_{1\le q\le Q}\sum_{a=1}^q E(x;q,a)^2.
\]

The inner sum includes every residue class, including the classes not
coprime to \(q\); there is no missing coprimality restriction. With power
parameter \(2\), the exponents in the lemma's first branch are

\[
 \frac22+\varepsilon=1+\varepsilon,\qquad
 2-\frac22=1.
\]

It follows that for each \(\varepsilon>0\) there is \(B_\varepsilon\)
such that

\[
 U(x,Q)\le B_\varepsilon x^{1+\varepsilon}Q
       \qquad(1\le Q\le x).                                \tag{20}
\]

The statement was checked both in the text extraction and in a rendered
image of the relevant supplied PDF page.

**5. Disposal of the initial moduli.** Let \(z\ge1\) be real, set
\(Z=f(z)\le x\), and use the definition \(V_f(x,z)\) in `problem.md`.
For each of the \(\lfloor z\rfloor\) indices in this sum, (1) gives the
weight bound

\[
 0<f'(k)\le Bz^{d-1}\le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha.                \tag{21}
\]

Moreover, \(f'(t)\ge1\) implies
\(f(k+1)-f(k)=\int_k^{k+1}f'(t)\,dt\ge1\). Hence the integers \(f(k)\)
are distinct positive moduli, and all those with \(k\le z\) are at most
\(Z\). Each residue-class variance is nonnegative. Before summing in \(k\),
(21) bounds its weighted value by \(BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha\) times the
corresponding unweighted variance. After summing its \(\lfloor z\rfloor\)
terms and enlarging to the \(\lfloor Z\rfloor\) possible positive moduli,
we obtain

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha
       \sum_{1\le q\le Z}\sum_{l=1}^q E(x;q,l)^2
 =BA^{-\alpha}Z^\alpha U(x,Z).                              \tag{22}
\]

To apply (20) here, \(x\ge2\) is positive, \(Q=Z=f(z)\ge2\) is a
positive real number, \(1\le Q\le x\) is part of the present hypotheses,
the power parameter is the integer \(2\ge2\), and the error parameter is
the prescribed \(\varepsilon>0\). These check every hypothesis of the
quoted lemma for this application. Equations (20) and (22) yield

\[
 0\le V_f(x,z)
 \le BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}Z^{1+\alpha}
 =BA^{-\alpha}B_\varepsilon
       x^{1+\varepsilon}f(z)^{2-1/d}.                        \tag{23}
\]

Taking a common constant larger than the constants in (19) and (23)
proves both assertions of P2, uniformly in all the stated ranges.

**Source and verification notes.** R. C. Vaughan, *A variance for k-free
numbers in arithmetic progressions* (2005), *Proceedings of the London
Mathematical Society* (3) **91**, 573--597,
[DOI:10.1112/S0024611505015352](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0024611505015352),
was consulted as a bibliographical pointer to the 1998 lemma. The estimate
used in the proof is the verbatim lemma quoted above from the supplied
1998 paper. A bibliographical web search returned post-2010 sources;
reading stopped when their dates were identified, and their content was
excluded from the argument.

A Python sanity check tested (9) and the exact identity (12) for all
integers \(1\le q\le\lfloor x\rfloor\), with
\(x\in\{2,3.25,10,31.75,100,200.5\}\), comprising 346 pairs \((x,q)\).
It used direct squarefree counts and the density formula of P1. Identity
(12) agreed within floating-point tolerance, and every test satisfied
(9). These computations serve only as checks; the proofs of (9) and
(12) are the finite identities and inequalities above.
=========== P3 statement
# P3: Uniform correlation estimate for squarefree numbers

For real x≥2 and every integer 1≤m≤x, define C_x(m)=Σ_{1≤n≤x−m}μ²(n)μ²(n+m) and 𝔖(m)=∏_p(1−2/p²)∏_{p²|m}(p²−1)/(p²−2), with products over primes. For every ε>0 there is C(ε)>0 such that |C_x(m)−(x−m)𝔖(m)|≤C(ε)x^(4/5+ε), uniformly for all such x and m. A permitted circle-method cutoff is Q=x^(2/5), for x sufficiently large that Q≤x^(1/2)/2; the major arcs are the subsets of R/Z with |α−a/q|≤Q/(qx), 1≤q≤Q and gcd(a,q)=1. The bound is uniform even when x−m is bounded.
=========== P3 proof
# Proof of P3

We prove the stronger bound
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|\le Kx^{4/5}
\tag{1}
\]
with an absolute constant \(K\), for all the parameters in the statement.
The argument is elementary and does not require a circle-method cutoff.
No external sources or results from the supplied papers are used, and the
dependency P1 is not needed. No numerical checks are used.

## An explicit divisor bound

Write \(\tau(n)\) for the number of positive divisors of a positive integer
\(n\). Define the absolute constant
\[
D=\prod_{p<2^{10}}(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2},
\]
where the product is over primes. We will use
\[
\tau(n)\le Dn^{1/10}\qquad(n\ge1).
\tag{2}
\]
Here is an elementary verification. For every integer \(a\ge0\),
\(a+1\le2^a\), as follows by induction. Consequently, if \(p\ge2^{10}\),
then \(a+1\le p^{a/10}\). If \(p<2^{10}\), the geometric-series identity gives
\[
(a+1)p^{-a/10}
\le\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}(j+1)p^{-j/10}
=(1-p^{-1/10})^{-2}.
\]
Multiplication over the prime powers in the factorization of \(n\) proves
(2); the factors included in \(D\) but absent from this factorization are
all at least one.

We also record the following bounds for positive real \(t\ge1\) and positive
integers \(H\):
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac1{j^2}\le2,\qquad
\sum_{j>H}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac1H,\qquad
\sum_{j>t}\frac1{j^2}\le\frac2t,\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{H}\frac1j\le1+\log H.
\tag{3}
\]
The first, second and fourth inequalities follow by comparison with the
integrals of \(u^{-2}\) and \(u^{-1}\). For the third, put \(k=\lfloor t\rfloor\).
Then \(k\ge t/2\), so the second inequality gives a bound \(1/k\le2/t\).

## Truncating the square-divisor identities

Fix real \(x\ge2\) and an integer \(1\le m\le x\), and put
\[
L=x-m\ge0,\qquad H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor.
\]
In particular,
\[
\tfrac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}.
\tag{4}
\]
For positive integers \(k\), define
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d\le H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d),\qquad
R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}\mu(d).
\]
All divisor variables in this proof are positive integers. The identity
\[
\mu^2(k)=\sum_{d^2\mid k}\mu(d)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)
\tag{5}
\]
follows by multiplying the local factors: a prime occurring to exponent at
least two contributes \(1+\mu(p)=0\); if no such prime occurs, the sum is one.
Also
\[
|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k),\qquad
|R_H(k)|\le\sum_{\substack{d>H\\d^2\mid k}}1.
\tag{6}
\]

For either of the two sets
\[
I_0=\{n:1\le n\le L\},\qquad
I_m=\{n+m:1\le n\le L\},
\]
there are \(\lfloor L\rfloor\) elements, all positive integers at most \(x\).
For each fixed \(d\), the number of elements divisible by \(d^2\) is at most
\(\lfloor x/d^2\rfloor\le x/d^2\). The outer sum below has
\(\max(0,\lfloor\sqrt x\rfloor-H)\le\sqrt x\) terms. Thus (3) and (6) give,
for each \(I\in\{I_0,I_m\}\),
\[
\sum_{k\in I}|R_H(k)|
\le\sum_{H<d\le\sqrt x}\frac{x}{d^2}
\le\frac{x}{H}.
\tag{7}
\]
This estimate also holds when either set is empty.

The exact product identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)
=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
and \(0\le\mu^2(k)\le1\) show that the absolute value of each summand is at
most
\[
|R_H(n)|+Dx^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|,
\]
where we used (2), (6), and \(n\le x\). Summing over the
\(\lfloor L\rfloor\le x\) admissible integers \(n\), and using (7) for
each of its two terms, yields
\[
\left|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\right|
\le (1+Dx^{1/10})\frac{x}{H}
\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}.
\tag{8}
\]
In particular this estimate has no inverse power of \(L\).

## Counting the truncated congruences

For \(d,e\le H\), set \(g=(d,e)\). The congruences
\[
n\equiv0\pmod{d^2},\qquad n\equiv-m\pmod{e^2}
\]
are soluble precisely when \(g^2\mid m\). Necessity follows by reducing
both congruences modulo \(g^2\). To verify sufficiency and the modulus of
the solutions, write \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\), where \((a,b)=1\), and write
\(n=d^2u\). If \(g^2\mid m\), the second congruence becomes
\[
a^2u\equiv -m/g^2\pmod{b^2}.
\]
Since \((a^2,b^2)=1\), this specifies one residue class of \(u\) modulo
\(b^2\), and hence one residue class of \(n\) modulo
\[
h=d^2b^2=\frac{d^2e^2}{g^2}.
\]
For any integer representative \(r\) of a residue class modulo \(h\), its
number of representatives in \(1\le n\le L\) is
\[
\left\lfloor\frac{L-r}{h}\right\rfloor
-\left\lfloor\frac{-r}{h}\right\rfloor
=\frac Lh+\theta,\qquad |\theta|\le1.
\tag{9}
\]
This formula is valid for every real \(L\ge0\).

Define
\[
A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\le H\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
Expanding the two finite divisor sums and applying (9) gives
\[
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=LA_H(m)+E_H,
\qquad |E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5}.
\tag{10}
\]
Indeed, the error for each compatible pair \((d,e)\) has absolute value
at most one after multiplication by \(\mu(d)\mu(e)\), and there are at
most \(H^2\) pairs. Incompatible pairs contribute zero.

## The infinite main term and its uniform tail

Consider
\[
A(m)=\sum_{\substack{d,e\ge1\\(d,e)^2\mid m}}
\frac{\mu(d)\mu(e)(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}.
\]
This series is absolutely convergent. In fact, writing \(d=ga\), \(e=gb\)
with \((a,b)=1\), and then dropping this coprimality condition, bounds its
absolute sum by
\[
\sum_{d,e\ge1}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
   \left(\sum_{a\ge1}\frac1{a^2}\right)
   \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right)
\le8.
\tag{11}
\]

We now bound the tail without using any restriction on the divisors of
\(m\). For the part with \(d>H\), the same change of variables gives
\[
\sum_{\substack{d>H\\e\ge1}}\frac{(d,e)^2}{d^2e^2}
\le\sum_{g\ge1}\frac1{g^2}
  \left(\sum_{a>H/g}\frac1{a^2}\right)
  \left(\sum_{b\ge1}\frac1{b^2}\right).
\tag{12}
\]
For a fixed \(g\le H\), the summand on the right of (12) is at most
\(g^{-2}(2g/H)\,2=4/(Hg)\), by (3). There are \(H\) such values of \(g\),
and their total is at most
\[
\frac4H\sum_{g=1}^{H}\frac1g
\le\frac{4(1+\log H)}H.
\]
For a fixed \(g>H\), both inner sums in (12) are at most two, giving
\(4/g^2\) before summing. The infinite sum over these \(g\) is at most
\(4/H\), by (3). Consequently the left side of (12) is at most
\((8+4\log H)/H\). The change of variables \((d,e)\mapsto(e,d)\) is a
bijection preserving the summand and carries the condition \(e>H\) to
\(d>H\), so the tail with \(e>H\) has exactly the same bound. The union
bound, together with \(|\mu(d)\mu(e)|\le1\), now gives
\[
|A(m)-A_H(m)|\le\frac{16+8\log H}{H}
=\frac{8(2+\log H)}H.
\tag{13}
\]
All sums used to obtain (13) were bounded after dropping
\((d,e)^2\mid m\), so its constant is independent of \(m\).

Absolute convergence in (11) permits factorization into prime factors:
one may first restrict both divisor variables to integers supported on a
finite set of primes and then let these sets exhaust the primes. Only
exponents zero and one occur in \(d,e\) because of the Möbius factors.
For a fixed prime \(p\), the choices of these two exponents contribute as
follows:

| Exponent in \(d\) | Exponent in \(e\) | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | \(1\) |
| 1 | 0 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 0 | 1 | \(-p^{-2}\) |
| 1 | 1 | \(p^{-2}\) if \(p^2\mid m\), and \(0\) otherwise |

It follows that
\[
\begin{aligned}
A(m)
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}
                   +\frac{\mathbf1_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\right)\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}
  \frac{1-p^{-2}}{1-2p^{-2}}\\
&=\prod_p\left(1-\frac2{p^2}\right)
  \prod_{p^2\mid m}\frac{p^2-1}{p^2-2}
=\mathfrak S(m).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
The second product is finite since \(m\ge1\). The first product converges
because \(\sum_p2p^{-2}<\infty\), and each of its factors is positive.

## Combining the bounds

Since \(0\le L\le x\), (4), (13), and (14) imply
\[
\begin{aligned}
L|A_H(m)-\mathfrak S(m)|
&\le\frac{8x(2+\log H)}H\\
&\le16x^{3/5}\left(2+\frac25\log x\right)\\
&=32x^{3/5}+\frac{32}{5}x^{3/5}\log x.
\end{aligned}
\tag{15}
\]
For \(x\ge1\),
\[
\log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}
\le\int_1^x t^{-4/5}\,dt
=5(x^{1/5}-1)\le5x^{1/5}.
\]
Thus (15) is at most
\[
32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\tag{16}
\]
Finally, (8), (10), and (16) give the fully explicit error bound
\[
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|C_x(m)-L\mathfrak S(m)\bigr|
&\le2x^{3/5}+2Dx^{7/10}+x^{4/5}+64x^{4/5}\\
&\le(67+2D)x^{4/5}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves (1). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), take
\(C(\varepsilon)=67+2D\) and use
\(x^{4/5}\le x^{4/5+\varepsilon}\). All bounds above hold for every
\(L\ge0\), including bounded \(L\) and \(L=0\), establishing the required
uniformity. \(\square\)

33	Also $f'(t)\geq 1$ and $f(1)\geq 2$ give $f(t)\geq t+1$. Thus $y<x$, and
34	\[
35	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
36	 \leq U\sum_{1\leq k\leq y}\frac1k
37	 \leq U(1+\log y)
38	 \leq 2U\log(2x).
39	 \tag{5}
40	\]
41	Here the sum has at most $\lfloor y\rfloor\leq\lfloor x\rfloor$ terms; the harmonic-sum bound follows by comparison with the integral of $1/t$ on $[1,y]$.
42	
43	We will use the following elementary lemma. If $b(k)$ is periodic of integer period $r\geq 1$, satisfies $|b(k)|\leq 1$, and has mean
44	\[
45	 m=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r b(a),
46	\]
47	then, for real $1\leq u\leq v$ and a continuously differentiable function $F$ on $[u,v]$,
48	\[
49	 \left|\sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^v F(t)\,dt\right|
50	 \leq 4r\left(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\,dt\right).
51	 \tag{6}
52	\]
53	To prove this, put
54	\[
55	 P(t)=\sum_{1\leq k\leq t}b(k)-mt.
56	\]
57	Writing $t=qr+s$, where $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\leq s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel. The remaining sum has at most $r$ terms of modulus at most $1$, and $|ms|\leq r$. Hence $|P(t)|\leq 2r$. Consequently
58	\[
59	 D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\leq t}b(k)-m(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)
60	 \quad\hbox{satisfies}\quad |D_u(t)|\leq 4r.
61	\]
62	Integration by parts gives the exact identity
63	\[
64	 \sum_{u<k\leq v}b(k)F(k)-m\int_u^vF(t)\,dt
65	 =F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\,dt,
66	\]
67	which proves (6), with the indicated convention at both endpoints.
68	
69	For later use, (4) and (6) yield
70	\[
71	 \left|\sum_{z<k\leq y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
72	       -m\log(Y/Z)\right|
73	 \leq \frac{4Dr}{z}.
74	 \tag{7}
75	\]
76	Indeed, $|w(y)|\leq U/z$, while
77	\(
78	\int_z^y |w'(t)|\,dt\leq V/z.
79	\)
80	These bounds also cover $z=y$; in that case the two conclusions of P4 are immediate. We may henceforth take $z<y$.

82	## Spectral notation and the common density
83	
84	Let $c_r(n)$, $\gamma(r)$, and $\lambda(r)$ have the meanings in P1. Since
85	\(
86	\lambda(r)=\varphi(r)\gamma(r)^2
87	\)
88	and $c_r(n)$ is a sum of $\varphi(r)$ complex numbers of modulus $1$,
89	\[
90	 |c_r(n)|\leq\varphi(r),\qquad
91	 \mathfrak S(n)=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)}.
92	 \tag{8}
93	\]
94	In particular, P1 gives absolute convergence, uniformly in $n\geq 1$, because $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
95	
96	For $h\geq 1$, define
97	\[
98	 \beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r
99	           \frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)}.
100	 \tag{9}
101	\]
102	Thus $|\beta_r(h)|\leq 1$, and
103	\[
104	 \mathcal W(h):=\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)
105	 \tag{10}
106	\]
107	converges absolutely and uniformly in $h\geq 1$. We now prove that
108	\[
109	 \mathcal W(h)=W_f(h).
110	 \tag{11}
111	\]
112	
113	For completeness, the elementary Ramanujan-sum identities needed here follow directly from finite sums. Inserting
114	\(
115	\mathbf 1_{(a,r)=1}=\sum_{b\mid(a,r)}\mu(b)
116	\)
117	into the definition of $c_r(n)$, and summing the resulting geometric progression, gives
118	\[
119	 c_r(n)
120	 =\sum_{b\mid r}\mu(b)
121	       \sum_{a'=1}^{r/b}\exp\!\left(\frac{2\pi i a'n}{r/b}\right)
122	 =\sum_{s\mid(r,n)}s\mu(r/s).
123	 \tag{12}
124	\]
125	Factoring this divisor sum over two coprime moduli shows that $c_{rs}(n)=c_r(n)c_s(n)$ when $(r,s)=1$. The Chinese remainder theorem, applied to the complete average in (9), therefore gives
126	\[
127	 \beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)\quad((r,s)=1).
128	 \tag{13}
129	\]
130	Here we also use $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$, which follows by counting invertible residue classes under the same bijection.
131	
132	The function $\lambda(r)/c^2$ is multiplicative, is supported on integers with no prime cube divisor, and has prime-power values
133	\[
134	 \frac{\lambda(p)}{c^2}=\frac{p-1}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
135	 \frac{\lambda(p^2)}{c^2}=\frac{p^2-p}{(p^2-1)^2}.
136	 \tag{14}
137	\]
138	The absolute convergence in (10) and (13)--(14) permit its Euler product. Equations (12) give, for each integer $n$,
139	\[
140	 c_p(n)=p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n}-1,
141	 \qquad
142	 c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-p\mathbf 1_{p\mid n},
143	\]
144	and hence
145	\[
146	 c_p(n)+c_{p^2}(n)=p^2\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}-1.
147	 \tag{15}
148	\]
149	Put
150	\[
151	 \delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
152	\]
153	The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ can also be taken modulo $p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. It follows from (14)--(15) that the local factor, before including the local factor of $c^2$, is
154	\[
155	 1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}
156	 =1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}.
157	 \tag{16}
158	\]
159	
160	Write $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$. If $j=2$, the condition is $p^2\mid f(a)$, so there are $\rho(p^2)$ classes modulo $p^2$. If $j=1$, the condition is $p\mid f(a)$, and each of its $\rho(p)$ classes modulo $p$ has $p$ lifts modulo $p^2$. If $j=0$, every class is allowed. Using $\rho(1)=1$, the three cases give
161	\[
162	 \delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^j)}{p^j},\qquad 0\leq\delta_p(h)\leq 1.
163	 \tag{17}
164	\]
165	No restriction on the coefficients of $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
166	
167	Unique factorization and the absolutely convergent geometric series for each prime give
168	\(
169	c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2.
170	\)
171	Multiplying (16) by its local factor gives the exact identity
172	\[
173	 \begin{aligned}
174	 (1-p^{-2})^2
175	 \left(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\right)
176	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}\\
177	 &=(1-2p^{-2})
178	       \left(1+\frac{\rho(p^{j_p(h)})}
179	       {p^{j_p(h)}(p^2-2)}\right).
180	 \end{aligned}
181	 \tag{18}
182	\]
183	This proves (11). All product rearrangements are absolute: the deviation from $1$ of the first expression on the right of (18) is at most $2/p^2$, and the added term in the second factor is at most
184	\(
185	1/(p^2-2)\leq 2/p^2.
186	\)
187	The sum of these bounds over primes is finite. This proves the asserted absolute convergence of $W_f(h)$. For the product defining $\mathfrak S(n)$, its local factor is
188	$1-2/p^2+\mathbf 1_{p^2\mid n}/p^2$, whose deviation from $1$ is at most $2/p^2$; its product therefore converges absolutely as well. Finally,
189	\[
190	 0\leq\frac{\rho(r)}r\leq 1,
191	 \qquad
192	 \sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
193	 \leq\sum_{r\geq 1}\lambda(r)=c,
194	 \tag{19}
195	\]
196	which proves absolute convergence of $R_f$.
197	
198	For real $R\geq 2$, set
199	\[
200	 L_R=(\log(2R))^2,\qquad
201	 T_R=\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r),\qquad
202	 M_R=\sum_{r\leq R}r\lambda(r).
203	\]
204	By P1 there is an absolute $C_0>0$ such that
205	\[
206	 T_R\leq C_0R^{-1/2}L_R,
207	 \qquad M_R\leq C_0R^{1/2}L_R.
208	 \tag{20}
209	\]

211	## The first averaging assertion
212	
213	For each positive integer $r$, the sequence
214	\(
215	b(k)=\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
216	\)
217	has period $r$, modulus at most $1$, and mean $\rho(r)/r$. Thus (7) gives
218	\[
219	 \sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\mathbf 1_{r\mid f(k)}
220	 =\frac{\rho(r)}r\log(Y/Z)+e_r,
221	 \qquad |e_r|\leq\frac{4Dr}{z}.
222	 \tag{21}
223	\]
224	The first identity for the squared densities in P1 applies to $q=f(k)$, which is a positive integer. Therefore, writing the expression to be estimated as $S_1$,
225	\[
226	 \begin{aligned}
227	 S_1
228	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}f'(k)\sum_{l=1}^{f(k)}g(f(k),l)^2\\
229	 &=\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
230	                     \sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
231	 \end{aligned}
232	 \tag{22}
233	\]
234	The part in (22) with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most
235	\[
236	 T_R\sum_{z<k\leq y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}
237	 \leq 2U T_R\log(2x)
238	 \tag{23}
239	\]
240	by (5). This uses at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$; before summing, the bound for each such value is $T_R f'(k)/f(k)\leq U T_R/k$.
241	
242	For $r\leq R$, there are $\lfloor R\rfloor$ indices. Before summing, the error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ in (21) is at most $4Dr\lambda(r)/z$. After summing it is at most $4DM_R/z$. Equations (21)--(23) consequently give
243	\[
244	 \left|S_1-\log(Y/Z)\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r\right|
245	 \leq\frac{4DM_R}{z}+2U T_R\log(2x).
246	 \tag{24}
247	\]
248	For the infinite omitted part of the density coefficient, (19) gives the bound $\lambda(r)\log(Y/Z)$ at each index $r>R$, and summing gives
249	\[
250	 \log(Y/Z)\sum_{r>R}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
251	 \leq T_R\log(2x),
252	 \tag{25}
253	\]
254	since $2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x$. As $Z\leq Bz^d$, we have
255	\(
256	z^{-1}\leq B^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}.
257	\)
258	Combining (20), (24), and (25) proves the explicit bound
259	\[
260	 \boxed{
261	 |S_1-R_f\log(Y/Z)|
262	 \leq C_0\left(
263	 4DB^{1/d} Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
264	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
265	 \right).}
266	 \tag{26}
267	\]

269	## A weight bound for the second assertion
270	
271	Let
272	\[
273	 H=\left\lfloor\frac{x}{Z}\right\rfloor.
274	\]
275	Since $f'(t)\geq 1$, $f$ has a continuous increasing inverse on $[f(1),\infty)$. For $1\leq h\leq H$, define
276	\[
277	 v_h=\min\{y,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad
278	 F_h(t)=f'(t)(x-hf(t))\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
279	 \tag{27}
280	\]
281	These definitions are valid because $x/h\geq Z=f(z)$. They give
282	\[
283	 z\leq v_h\leq (x/(ah))^{1/d},\qquad
284	 0\leq x-hf(t)\leq x\quad(z\leq t\leq v_h).
285	 \tag{28}
286	\]
287	Define a constant $K$ by
288	\[
289	 K=
290	 \begin{cases}
291	 B+B^2/a,&d=1,\\[2mm]
292	 B+B/(d-1)+B^2/((2d-1)a),&d\geq 2.
293	 \end{cases}
294	 \tag{29}
295	\]
296	We claim
297	\[
298	 |F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
299	 \leq Kxv_h^{d-1}.
300	 \tag{30}
301	\]
302	For $d\geq 2$, (1)--(2) and (28) give
303	\[
304	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bxv_h^{d-1},
305	\]
306	and
307	\[
308	 \begin{aligned}
309	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
310	 &\leq\int_z^{v_h}
311	       \left(|f''(t)|(x-hf(t))+h|f'(t)|^2\right)\,dt\\
312	 &\leq Bx\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\,dt
313	       +hB^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\,dt\\
314	 &\leq\frac{B}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}
315	       +\frac{hB^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1}\\
316	 &\leq\left(\frac{B}{d-1}+\frac{B^2}{(2d-1)a}\right)
317	          xv_h^{d-1}.
318	 \end{aligned}
319	 \tag{31}
320	\]
321	The last inequality uses $hv_h^d\leq x/a$, from (28). For $d=1$, $f''=0$ gives
322	\[
323	 |F_h(v_h)|\leq Bx,\qquad
324	 \int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\,dt
325	 \leq hB^2(v_h-z)\leq hB^2v_h\leq B^2x/a.
326	 \tag{32}
327	\]
328	Thus (30) holds for every $d\geq 1$.
329	
330	Apply (6) to
331	\(
332	b(k)=c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)
333	\)
334	with mean $\beta_r(h)$. This sequence has period $r$ because $f$ has integer coefficients. Equations (28)--(30) give
335	\[
336	 \begin{aligned}
337	 &\left|\sum_{z<k\leq v_h}
338	     f'(k)(x-hf(k))\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}
339	   -\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du\right|\\
340	 &\hspace{15mm}\leq
341	 4Kr x v_h^{d-1}
342	 \leq 4K a^{-(d-1)/d} r x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}.
343	 \end{aligned}
344	 \tag{33}
345	\]
346	If $v_h=z$, the left side is zero and this bound still applies.
347	
348	The $h$-sum has exactly $H\leq x/Z$ indices. The bound in (33) is the bound before summing. To sum it, the function $t^{-1+1/d}$ is nonincreasing and integrable on $(0,H]$, and therefore
349	\[
350	 \sum_{h=1}^{H}h^{-1+1/d}
351	 \leq\int_0^H t^{-1+1/d}\,dt
352	 =dH^{1/d}\leq d(x/Z)^{1/d}.
353	 \tag{34}
354	\]
355	This includes $d=1$, when the first inequality is equality. Combining (33)--(34), the error after summing over $h$ is at most
356	\[
357	 K_2 r x^2 Z^{-1/d},\qquad
358	 K_2=4Kd\,a^{-(d-1)/d}.
359	 \tag{35}
360	\]
361	In particular no logarithm is introduced by this sum.

363	## The second averaging assertion
364	
365	Define the finite approximations
366	\[
367	 \mathfrak S_R(n)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)
368	                         \frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad
369	 W_R(h)=\sum_{r\leq R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
370	\]
371	Equations (8)--(11) give, uniformly for positive integers $n,h$,
372	\[
373	 |\mathfrak S(n)-\mathfrak S_R(n)|\leq T_R,
374	 \qquad |W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\leq T_R.
375	 \tag{36}
376	\]
377	
378	Let $S_2$ denote the discrete expression in the second assertion and $I_2$ its integral expression. Define $S_{2,R}$ and $I_{2,R}$ by replacing $\mathfrak S$ and $W_f$ with $\mathfrak S_R$ and $W_R$, respectively.
379	
380	For a fixed integer $k$ with $z<k\leq y$, there are
381	\(
382	H_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\leq x/f(k)
383	\)
384	indices $h$. Before summing over $h$, the error from (36) is at most $T_R f'(k)(x-hf(k))\leq T_R x f'(k)$. After summing over these $H_k$ indices, it is at most
385	\(
386	T_R x^2 f'(k)/f(k).
387	\)
388	Summing this last bound over at most $\lfloor y\rfloor$ values of $k$ and using (5) gives
389	\[
390	 |S_2-S_{2,R}|\leq 2U T_R x^2\log(2x).
391	 \tag{37}
392	\]
393	For each $t\in[Z,Y]$, the $h$-sum has $\lfloor x/t\rfloor\leq x/t$ indices. Before summing, the error in an integrand term is at most $T_R(x-ht)\leq T_R x$. After summing it is at most $T_R x^2/t$. Integration gives
394	\[
395	 |I_2-I_{2,R}|
396	 \leq T_R x^2\int_Z^Y\frac{dt}{t}
397	 =T_R x^2\log(Y/Z)
398	 \leq T_R x^2\log(2x).
399	 \tag{38}
400	\]
401	
402	It remains to compare the finite approximations. All relevant sums are finite, so their orders can be interchanged. The change of variables $t=f(u)$ gives, for each $h\leq H$,
403	\[
404	 \int_z^{v_h}f'(u)(x-hf(u))\,du
405	 =\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\,dt.
406	 \tag{39}
407	\]
408	Moreover, for integer $k$ in $(z,y]$, the condition $h\leq x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\leq v_h$. Thus (35) compares the entire $h$-sum at a fixed $r$ in $S_{2,R}$ with its counterpart in $I_{2,R}$. Before summing over $r$, its error after multiplication by $\lambda(r)$ is at most
409	\(
410	K_2r\lambda(r)x^2 Z^{-1/d}.

413	\[
414	 |S_{2,R}-I_{2,R}|
415	 \leq K_2x^2Z^{-1/d}M_R

420	\[
421	 \boxed{
422	 |S_2-I_2|
423	 \leq C_0 x^2\left(
424	 K_2 Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}L_R
425	 +(2U+1)R^{-1/2}L_R\log(2x)
426	 \right).}

428	\]

431	\[
432	 C(f)=C_0\max\{4DB^{1/d},\ K_2,\ 2U+1\}.
433	\]
434	With $A$ as in the statement, (26) is the first asserted inequality with right side $C(f)A$, and (41) is the second with right side $C(f)x^2A$. All constants are independent of $x,z,y,R$. 441	=========== P5 proof
442	Put \(A_d=[t^d]f(t)\ne0\), and fix
443	\[
444	C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|,1\}.
445	\]
446	For every prime \(p\nmid A_d\), reduction modulo \(p\) is a nonzero
447	polynomial of degree \(d\), so the factor theorem gives at most \(d\)
448	roots. If \(p\mid A_d\), the bound
449	\(\rho(p)\le p\le |A_d|\) applies. Each residue class modulo \(p\) has
450	exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\). Consequently,
451	\[
452	0\le\rho(p)\le\min\{C_0,p\},\qquad
453	0\le\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)\le C_0p.                 \tag{1}
454	\]
455	These bounds require no assumption on the content, discriminant, or
456	factorization of \(f\).
457	
458	We will use the following explicit summation estimate. If \(u>1\) and
459	\(N\ge1\) is an integer, comparison with an integral gives
460	\[
461	\sum_{p>N}p^{-u}\le\sum_{n>N}n^{-u}
462	\le\int_N^\infty t^{-u}\,dt
463	=\frac{N^{1-u}}{u-1}.                              \tag{2}
464	\]
465	Both sums in (2) have infinitely many possible indices. A bound
466	\(k p^{-u}\) for each prime therefore has total at most
467	\(kN^{1-u}/(u-1)\) after summing over \(p>N\). In particular, the sum over
468	all primes is at most \(k/(u-1)\).
469	If local factors are \(1+e_p(s)\), the estimate
470	\[
471	\left|\prod_{p>N}(1+e_p(s))-1\right|
472	\le \exp\!\left(\sum_{p>N}|e_p(s)|\right)-1          \tag{3}
473	\]
474	follows first for finite products by expansion and then for their limits.
475	Thus all the prime-sum tail estimates below also give explicit product
476	tail estimates. Uniform summability of \(|e_p|\) on compact sets gives
477	local uniform convergence to a holomorphic function, since the finite
478	products are holomorphic.
479	
480	For brevity put \(q_p=1-2/p^2\), and introduce the three coefficients
481	\[
482	\begin{aligned}
483	\alpha_p&=q_pa_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
484	\beta_p&=q_p(b_p-a_p)=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}
485	                              -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\\
486	\delta_p&=q_p(c_p-b_p)=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
487	\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{4}
488	\]
489	By (1),
490	\[
491	\begin{gathered}
492	0<q_p\le\alpha_p\le1,\qquad
493	0\le\beta_p\le C_0p^{-3},\qquad
494	0\le\delta_p\le p^{-2},\\
495	|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3},\qquad
496	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}.                 \tag{5}
497	\end{gathered}
498	\]
499	In particular, \(b_p-a_p\ge0\) and \(c_p-b_p\ge0\).
500	
501	The local factor \(w_p(h)\) in \(W_f(h)\) is, according as
502	\(v_p(h)=0,1\) or at least \(2\),
503	\[
504	w_p(h)=\alpha_p,\quad
505	\alpha_p+\beta_p,\quad
506	\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p,
507	\]
508	respectively. Alternatively, the elementary bound
509	\(0\le\rho(p^j)\le p^j\), including \(j=0\), gives directly
510	\[
511	1-\frac2{p^2}\le w_p(h)\le1-\frac1{p^2},\qquad
512	|w_p(h)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}.                          \tag{6}
513	\]
514	The prime tail of the last bound is at most \(2/N\) by (2), uniformly
515	in \(h\). Every factor is at least \(1/2\). For \(1/2\le t\le1\),
516	\(-\log t\le2(1-t)\); hence
517	\[
518	\sum_p|\log w_p(h)|\le4\sum_pp^{-2}\le4.
519	\]
520	It follows that the product defining \(W_f(h)\) is absolutely convergent
521	and \(0<W_f(h)\le1\). For \(s=\sigma+it\) with \(\sigma>1\), this gives
522	\[
523	\sum_{h\ge1}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_{h\ge1}h^{-\sigma}<\infty.
524	\]
525	More explicitly, the sum of the errors over the infinitely many indices
526	\(h>N\) is bounded by
527	\[
528	\sum_{h>N}|W_f(h)h^{-s}|
529	\le\sum_{h>N}h^{-\sigma}
530	\le\frac{N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                  \tag{7}
531	\]
532	This proves the asserted absolute convergence of \(D_f\).
533	
534	Write
535	\[
536	L_p(s)=q_pB_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s}.
537	\]
538	On the closed half-plane \(\Re s\ge\sigma\), (5) gives the bound for
539	each individual prime
540	\[
541	|L_p(s)-1|
542	\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}.       \tag{8}
543	\]
544	If \(\sigma>-1/2\), all four exponents exceed \(1\). Summing (8) over
545	the infinitely many primes \(p>N\), using (2) separately for its four
546	terms, yields
547	\[
548	\begin{aligned}
549	\sum_{p>N}|L_p(s)-1|\le E_P(N;\sigma)
550	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
551	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
552	 +\frac{N^{-1-2\sigma}}{1+2\sigma}.                 \tag{9}
553	\end{aligned}
554	\]
555	Every power of \(N\) on the right has negative exponent. Equations
556	(3) and (9) prove absolute and locally uniform convergence of \(P_f\)
557	on \(\Re s>-1/2\). They also prove its holomorphy there.
558	
559	The local factor in \(H_f\) is
560	\[
561	\begin{aligned}
562	M_p(s)&=(1-p^{-2s-2})L_p(s)\\
563	 &=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}
564	 +(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2})p^{-2s}
565	 -\beta_pp^{-2}p^{-3s}-\delta_pp^{-2}p^{-4s}.         \tag{10}
566	\end{aligned}
567	\]
568	The coefficient where cancellation is needed is exactly
569	\[
570	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}
571	 =-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}
572	                         -\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6},
573	\]
574	so its absolute value is at most
575	\(C_0p^{-3}+2p^{-4}+C_0p^{-5}\). Thus, for \(\Re s\ge\sigma\),
576	\[
577	\begin{aligned}
578	|M_p(s)-1|\le{}&2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}
579	 +C_0p^{-3-2\sigma}+2p^{-4-2\sigma}\\
580	 &+C_0p^{-5-2\sigma}+C_0p^{-5-3\sigma}
581	 +p^{-4-4\sigma}.                                  \tag{11}
582	\end{aligned}
583	\]
584	For \(\sigma>-3/4\), the eight exponents on the right are, respectively,
585	\[
586	2,\ 3,\ 3+\sigma,\ 3+2\sigma,\ 4+2\sigma,
587	\ 5+2\sigma,\ 5+3\sigma,\ 4+4\sigma,
588	\]
589	and each is greater than \(1\). The sum over the infinitely many primes
590	\(p>N\), before summation bounded prime by prime by (11), is after
591	summation bounded by
592	\[
593	\begin{aligned}
594	\sum_{p>N}|M_p(s)-1|\le E_H(N;\sigma)
595	={}&\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}
596	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-\sigma}}{2+\sigma}
597	 +\frac{C_0N^{-2-2\sigma}}{2+2\sigma}\\
598	 &+\frac{2N^{-3-2\sigma}}{3+2\sigma}
599	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-2\sigma}}{4+2\sigma}
600	 +\frac{C_0N^{-4-3\sigma}}{4+3\sigma}
601	 +\frac{N^{-3-4\sigma}}{3+4\sigma}.                 \tag{12}
602	\end{aligned}
603	\]
604	All denominators in (12) are positive, and all powers of \(N\) have
605	negative exponents in this range. Equations (3) and (12) prove absolute
606	and locally uniform convergence, and holomorphy, of \(H_f\) on
607	\(\Re s>-3/4\). For every real \(t\), the bound
608	\(|M_p(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(|M_p(\sigma+it)-1|)\) also proves
609	\[
610	|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le \exp(E_H(1;\sigma)).             \tag{13}
611	\]
612	Thus one may take \(C(f,\sigma)=\exp(E_H(1;\sigma))\), with every
613	term in its exponent specified in (12).
614	
615	We next identify the Dirichlet series. The positive number
616	\[
617	A=\prod_p\alpha_p
618	\]
619	exists by (5), or by (6) with \(h=1\). Define
620	\(u(h)=W_f(h)/A\). Only the primes dividing \(h\) change a factor of
621	this quotient, so \(u\) is multiplicative and
622	\[
623	u(1)=1,\qquad u(p)=\frac{b_p}{a_p},\qquad
624	u(p^e)=\frac{c_p}{a_p}\quad(e\ge2).
625	\]
626	In particular \(0<u(h)\le A^{-1}\). For \(\Re s>1\), its local series is
627	\[
628	\sum_{e\ge0}u(p^e)p^{-es}
629	 =1+\frac{b_p}{a_p}p^{-s}
630	       +\frac{c_p}{a_p}\frac{p^{-2s}}{1-p^{-s}}
631	 =\frac{B_p(s)}{a_p(1-p^{-s})}.                    \tag{14}
632	\]
633	To justify multiplication of these series, first include only primes
634	\(p\le N\). Their finite product expands into the sum over integers
635	whose prime factors are all at most \(N\). Every omitted integer is
636	greater than \(N\). The omitted sum has infinitely many possible
637	indices, each term has modulus at most \(A^{-1}h^{-\sigma}\), and its
638	total modulus is at most
639	\[
640	\frac{A^{-1}N^{1-\sigma}}{\sigma-1}.                \tag{15}
641	\]
642	This tends to zero. Multiplying (14) over all primes therefore gives
643	\[
644	\begin{aligned}
645	D_f(s)
646	 &=\lim_{N\to\infty}
647	 \left(\prod_{p\le N}\frac{L_p(s)}{1-p^{-s}}\right)
648	 \left(\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p\right)\\
649	 &=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad \Re s>1.                 \tag{16}
650	\end{aligned}
651	\]
652	Here the Euler product for \(\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}\) follows
653	by unique prime factorization: its finite-prime expansion omits only
654	integers \(n>N\), whose total absolute contribution is at most
655	\(N^{1-\sigma}/(\sigma-1)\). The extra tail product in (16) tends to
656	\(1\), with explicit bound
657	\[
658	\left|\prod_{p>N}\alpha_p-1\right|
659	 \le \exp\!\left(\frac2N+\frac{C_0}{2N^2}\right)-1. \tag{17}
660	\]
661	
662	For \(\Re s>-1/2\), the Euler product for \(\zeta(2s+2)\) is
663	absolutely convergent. Its reciprocal product is nonzero, since
664	\(|p^{-2s-2}|<1\) and
665	\(\sum_p|p^{-2s-2}|<\infty\). Multiplying the absolutely convergent
666	products defining \(P_f\) and \(H_f\) gives
667	\[
668	P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\quad(\Re s>-1/2).          \tag{18}
669	\]
670	In particular, (16) proves both required identities on \(\Re s>1\).
671	
672	For completeness, the zeta-function facts needed for continuation and
673	signs can all be derived directly. For \(\Re w>1\), integrating the
674	counting function of the positive integers gives
675	\[
676	\zeta(w)=w\int_1^\infty\lfloor x\rfloor x^{-w-1}\,dx
677	 =\frac1{w-1}+\frac12
678	       -w\int_1^\infty(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx.     \tag{19}
679	\]
680	Let
681	\(\mathcal B_2(x)=\{x\}^2-\{x\}+1/6\).
682	This function is continuous at integers, is bounded in absolute value
683	by \(1/6\), and has derivative \(2(\{x\}-1/2)\) between consecutive
684	integers. More explicitly, for an integer \(T\ge2\), integration by
685	parts over the \(T-1\) intervals between \(1\) and \(T\) gives the
686	exact identity
687	\[
688	\int_1^T(\{x\}-1/2)x^{-w-1}\,dx
689	 =\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}
690	  +\frac{w+1}{2}\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.
691	\]
692	The internal endpoint terms cancel exactly. The upper endpoint
693	term, after multiplication by \(-w\), has modulus
694	\(|w|T^{-\Re w-1}/12\), which tends to zero for \(\Re w>1\).
695	Substitution in (19) therefore yields
696	\[
697	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}
698	 -\frac{w(w+1)}2
699	       \int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-w-2}\,dx.    \tag{20}
700	\]
701	The integral is holomorphic for \(\Re w>-1\). Explicitly, its tail
702	past \(T\ge1\), including the coefficient in (20), has absolute value
703	at most
704	\[
705	\frac{|w(w+1)|}{12(\Re w+1)}T^{-\Re w-1}.           \tag{21}
706	\]
707	For each nonnegative integer \(m\), the \(m\)-th derivative of the
708	integrand with respect to \(w\) is dominated on \(\Re w\ge\eta>-1\)
709	by \((\log x)^m x^{-\eta-2}/6\), whose integral is
710	\(m!/[6(\eta+1)^{m+1}]\). These bounds justify holomorphy and the
711	continuation in (20), with its sole pole at \(w=1\) and residue \(1\).
712	
713	We also record the constant term at that pole. For an integer \(N\ge1\),
714	the same counting-function integration gives, initially for
715	\(\Re w>1\) and then by continuation for \(\Re w>0\),
716	\[
717	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n=1}^N n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}
718	       -w\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-w-1}\,dx.           \tag{22}
719	\]
720	The finite sum has exactly \(N\) terms. The final integral, including
721	its coefficient, is bounded by
722	\(|w|N^{-\Re w}/\Re w\). Subtracting \(1/(w-1)\) and taking
723	\(w\to1\) gives
724	\[
725	\lim_{w\to1}\left(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\right)
726	 =\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n-\log N
727	       -\int_N^\infty\{x\}x^{-2}\,dx.
728	\]
729	The integral is between \(0\) and \(1/N\). Taking \(N\to\infty\),
730	the right side is Euler's constant \(\gamma_E\), by its defining
731	harmonic-sum limit.
732	
733	Equation (20) gives \(\zeta(0)=-1/2\). At \(w=-1/2\) it gives
734	\[
735	\zeta(-1/2)=-\frac5{24}
736	       +\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(x)x^{-3/2}\,dx.
737	\]
738	The integral has absolute value at most
739	\((1/6)\int_1^\infty x^{-3/2}\,dx=1/3\). Hence
740	\[
741	-\frac14\le\zeta(-1/2)\le-\frac16<0.              \tag{23}
742	\]
743	
744	For \(\Re s>-3/4\), the two arguments \(s\) and \(2s+2\) in
745	\[
746	\widetilde D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)         \tag{24}
747	\]
748	satisfy \(\Re s>-1\) and \(\Re(2s+2)>1/2>-1\).
749	Thus (20) and the holomorphy of \(H_f\) prove that (24) is
750	meromorphic throughout this region. It agrees with \(D_f\) on
751	\(\Re s>1\) by (16) and (18), so it is the claimed continuation.
752	We henceforth use the notation \(D_f\) for this continuation.
753	
754	At \(s=0\),
755	\[
756	L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2},\qquad
757	P_f(0)=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})=\frac1{\zeta(2)}.
758	\]
759	The equality \(D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)\) extends meromorphically to
760	\(\Re s>-1/2\) by (18) and (24). Both factors are regular at zero,
761	so
762	\[
763	D_f(0)=\zeta(0)P_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}.          \tag{25}
764	\]
765	
766	At \(s=1\), \(P_f\) is holomorphic. With \(R_f=P_f(1)\), equations
767	(16) and (22) show
768	\[
769	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=1}D_f(s)=R_f,\qquad
770	\lim_{s\to1}\left(D_f(s)-\frac{R_f}{s-1}\right)
771	 =\gamma_ER_f+P_f'(1)=B_f+\frac32R_f.               \tag{26}
772	\]
773	This proves that the definitions of \(R_f\) and \(B_f\) have the
774	specified values without any unspecified remainder in a Laurent
775	expansion.
776	
777	At \(s=-1/2\), every local factor of \(H_f\) is strictly positive:
778	\[
779	M_p(-1/2)
780	 =(1-p^{-1})\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)>0. \tag{27}
781	\]
782	The nonnegativity and strict positivity needed here are exactly (5).
783	The series of absolute deviations of these factors from \(1\)
784	converges by (11)--(12) with \(\sigma=-1/2\). A convergent product
785	of positive factors with summable absolute deviations has positive
786	limit: after finitely many factors, \(|M_p(-1/2)-1|\le1/2\), and
787	then \(|\log M_p(-1/2)|\le2|M_p(-1/2)-1|\).
788	Consequently \(H_f(-1/2)>0\). Combining this with (23) proves
789	\[
790	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)>0.                \tag{28}
791	\]
792	For clarity, the explicit Euler product in this constant is
793	\[
794	K_f=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)
795	 \prod_p\left\{
796	 (1-2/p^2)(1-1/p)
797	 \bigl[a_p+(b_p-a_p)\sqrt p+(c_p-b_p)p\bigr]
798	 \right\}.                                       \tag{29}
799	\]
800	The factors inside braces are kept grouped at each prime; their
801	absolute convergence is precisely the convergence just proved for
802	\(H_f(-1/2)\). The pole of \(\zeta(2s+2)\) contributes a factor
803	\(1/2\) to its residue. Equations (23)--(24) therefore also give
804	\[
805	\operatorname*{Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
806	 =\frac12\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2)=-\frac3{16}K_f.       \tag{30}
807	\]
808	The only possible poles in the stated region are \(1\) and \(-1/2\).
809	Both are genuine: the local factors of \(P_f(1)\) are positive with
810	summable absolute deviations, and (28) makes (30) nonzero.
811	
812	It remains to identify the common density coefficient. Substitution
813	of (4) into \(L_p(1)\) gives the exact identity
814	\[
815	\begin{aligned}
816	L_p(1)
817	 &=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}{p}+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}\\
818	 &=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}
819	       +\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}\\
820	 &=(1-p^{-2})^2
821	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right].
822	                                                               \tag{31}
823	\end{aligned}
824	\]
825	Let
826	\[
827	T_p=\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}.
828	\]
829	Since \(p^2-1\ge3p^2/4\), (1) bounds the term for each prime by
830	\[
831	0\le T_p\le\frac{16C_0}{9}(p^{-4}+p^{-3}).          \tag{32}
832	\]
833	The sum over the infinitely many primes \(p>N\) is therefore bounded
834	explicitly by
835	\[
836	\sum_{p>N}T_p
837	 \le\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right). \tag{33}
838	\]
839	This proves absolute convergence of the product of \(1+T_p\).
840	The product of \((1-p^{-2})^2\) is absolutely convergent as well,
841	since the absolute deviation of its factor from \(1\) is
842	\(2p^{-2}-p^{-4}\le2p^{-2}\), with prime tail at most \(2/N\).
843	Multiplying (31) over the primes and using the Euler product for
844	\(\zeta(2)\) proves
845	\[
846	R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p
847	 \left[1+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{(p^2-1)^2}\right]. \tag{34}
848	\]
849	
850	Finally, the Chinese remainder theorem gives
851	\(\rho(mn)=\rho(m)\rho(n)\) for \((m,n)=1\): the bijection between
852	residues modulo \(mn\) and pairs of residues modulo \(m,n\) restricts
853	to a bijection between the respective polynomial roots. Put
854	\[
855	v(r)=
856	\begin{cases}
857	\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(r)\rho(r)}r
858	             \prod_{p\mid r}(p^2-1)^{-2},
859	 &\text{if no prime cube divides }r,\\
860	0,&\text{otherwise}.
861	\end{cases}
862	\]
863	This is a nonnegative multiplicative function with \(v(1)=1\).
864	Its first two prime-power values are
865	\[
866	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad
867	v(p^2)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2}.          \tag{35}
868	\]
869	For \(e\ge3\), its value \(v(p^e)\) is zero.
870	For the primes at most \(N\), the finite product of
871	\(1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p\) expands into a finite nonnegative sum over
872	the \(3^{\pi(N)}\) integers obtained by choosing each such prime's
873	exponent from \(\{0,1,2\}\). These sets increase to all integers
874	with no prime-cube divisor. By (32) and (2), their sums are bounded
875	by
876	\[
877	\prod_p(1+T_p)\le
878	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}\left(\frac13+\frac12\right)\right)
879	 =\exp(40C_0/27).                                  \tag{36}
880	\]
881	Monotone convergence thus proves absolute convergence and the
882	Euler-product identity
883	\[
884	\sum_{r\ge1}v(r)=\prod_p(1+T_p).
885	\]
886	Explicitly, the omitted sum over the infinitely many integers having
887	a prime divisor greater than \(N\) is at most
888	\[
889	\exp(40C_0/27)
890	 \left[
891	 \exp\!\left(\frac{16C_0}{9}
892	                \left(\frac1{3N^3}+\frac1{2N^2}\right)\right)-1
893	 \right].                                         \tag{37}
894	\]
895	Indeed the omitted sum is exactly
896	\[
897	\left(\prod_{p\le N}(1+T_p)\right)
898	\left(\prod_{p>N}(1+T_p)-1\right),
899	\]
900	so (3), (33), and (36) give (37).
901	The definition of \(\lambda(r)\) in the statement satisfies
902	\(\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=\zeta(2)^{-2}v(r)\). Equations (34)--(35)
903	therefore give the required identity
904	\[
905	R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
906	\]
907	All the Euler products specifying \(R_f\) or \(K_f\) have had their
908	absolute convergence established above.
909	
910	No external literature or numerical checks were used in this proof.
911
