=========== P6 proof
# Proof of P6

We use P5 as a black box, with the notation in `statement.md` and
`deps/P5.md`. In particular,
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)\qquad(\Re s>-3/4),
\tag{1}
\]
as an identity of meromorphic functions. The Euler product defining
\(H_f\) is holomorphic in this half-plane. All constants constructed below
are independent of the real variable \(H\geq1\).

## 1. The external statements used

The only external source used is H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan,
*Multiplicative Number Theory I. Classical Theory* (2007), Chapter 10,
pp. 329–330, [doi:10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314.012),
as supplied in
`papers/montgomery-vaughan-2007/analytic_properties_of_the_zeta_function_and_lfunctions.pdf`.
Here are the two statements used, quoted verbatim, with mathematical
typesetting transcribed from the PDF.

> **Corollary 10.4** For all \(s\ne1\),
> \[
> \zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin\frac{\pi s}{2}.
> \tag{10.9}
> \]

> **Corollary 10.5** Suppose that \(A>0\) is fixed. Then
> \[
> |\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|
> \]
> uniformly for \(|\sigma|\leq A\) and \(|t|\geq1\). Here
> \(\tau=|t|+4\), as usual.

Both quotations were checked against rendered pages of the supplied PDF.
For Corollary 10.4 we will only need \(-5/8\leq\Re s<0\) and a
neighborhood of zero. These points satisfy \(s\ne1\). In the negative
strip \(\Re(1-s)>1\), so \(\zeta(1-s)\) is analytic there;
\(\Gamma(1-s)\) is analytic there because its argument has positive real
part. At zero, the pole of \(\zeta(1-s)\) is canceled by
\(\sin(\pi s/2)\). Thus \(\zeta(s)\) is analytic in the negative strip
and at zero. In the positive half-plane its only pole is the simple pole
at one with residue one; this also follows directly from (3) below.

For Corollary 10.5 we fix \(A=2\), and use it only when
\(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\) and \(|t|\geq2\). Hence \(A>0\),
\(|\sigma|\leq A\), and \(|t|\geq1\) all hold throughout its use.
Let \(Q>0\) be a constant such that its upper inequality reads
\[
|\zeta(\sigma+it)|
\leq Q(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-\sigma-it)|
\tag{2}
\]
in this range. No conditional estimate for zeta is used.

## 2. Bounds throughout the contour strip

We first derive a positive-half-plane estimate, including its dependence
on the imaginary part. For an integer \(N\geq1\), partial summation of
the tail of the defining series gives, initially for \(\Re s>1\),
\[
\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-s}
       +\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}
       -s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, write the tail as \(\int_N^\infty u^{-s}\,d\lfloor u\rfloor\),
replace \(\lfloor u\rfloor\) by \(u-\{u\}\), and integrate the second
term by parts. The boundary term at \(N\) vanishes because \(N\) is an
integer. The integral in (3) converges locally uniformly for
\(\Re s>0\), since \(0\leq\{u\}<1\); hence (3) holds there by analytic
continuation, away from \(s=1\). It also shows that the residue at one is
one and that there are no other poles in that half-plane.

Let \(s=\alpha+iv\), \(V=|v|\geq2\),
\(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6\), and \(\delta\in\{1/4,3/4\}\). Choose
\(N=\lceil V\rceil\), so \(V\leq N\leq3V/2\). The finite sum in (3)
has exactly \(N\) terms. Each term has modulus at most \(n^{-\delta}\),
and after summation its modulus is at most
\[
\sum_{n\leq N}n^{-\delta}
\leq1+\int_1^N u^{-\delta}\,du
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}
\leq\frac{(3/2)^{1-\delta}}{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}.
\]
The other two terms satisfy
\[
\left|\frac{N^{1-s}}{s-1}\right|
\leq\frac{N^{1-\delta}}{V}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq(3/2)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}
\]
and
\[
\left|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\,du\right|
\leq\frac{|s|}{\alpha}N^{-\alpha}
\leq\frac{V+6}{\delta}V^{-\delta}
\leq\frac4\delta V^{1-\delta}.
\]
Consequently, with the explicit constants
\[
C_\delta=(3/2)^{1-\delta}
              \left(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\right)+\frac4\delta,
\]
we have
\[
|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\leq C_\delta V^{1-\delta}
\quad(\delta\leq\alpha\leq6,\ V\geq2).
\tag{4}
\]

Now put \(s=\sigma+it\), \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2\), and \(T=|t|\geq2\).
For \(1/4\leq\sigma\leq2\), (4) with \(\delta=1/4\) gives
\[
|\zeta(s)|\leq C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\leq C_{1/4}T^{11/8}.
\]
For \(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq1/4\), the real part of \(1-s\) lies in
\([3/4,13/8]\), so (4) with \(\delta=3/4\), followed by (2), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\zeta(s)|
&\leq Q(T+4)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\\
&\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{3/4-\sigma}
\leq Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(T+4\leq3T\) and \(1/4\leq1/2-\sigma\leq9/8\).
Also \(3/4\leq\Re(2s+2)\leq6\), and its imaginary part has modulus
\(2T\geq4\). Thus
\[
|\zeta(2s+2)|\leq C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4}.
\tag{5}
\]

We next obtain a bound for \(H_f(s)\) uniform on this whole strip.
This is a uniformity supplement to the fixed-line bound in P5; we do not
need to strengthen its domain of continuation. Write \(d=\deg f\), and
let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient
of \(f\). For \(p\notin\mathcal B\), its reduction is a nonzero
polynomial over \(\mathbb F_p\), with at most \(d\) roots. Each residue
modulo \(p\) has exactly \(p\) lifts modulo \(p^2\), whence
\[
0\leq\rho(p)\leq d,\qquad0\leq\rho(p^2)\leq dp.
\tag{6}
\]
Use the quantities \(a_p,b_p,c_p\) defined in P5, and put
\(u_p=b_p-a_p\), \(q_p=c_p-b_p\). Since \(p^2-2\geq p^2/2\), (6)
gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
|a_p-1|\leq2dp^{-3},\qquad |u_p|\leq4dp^{-3},
\qquad |q_p|\leq(d+2)p^{-2},\\
|q_p-p^{-2}|\leq(2+2d)p^{-3},
\qquad |q_p-a_pp^{-2}|\leq(2+4d)p^{-3},\\
|(1-2p^{-2})a_p-1|\leq(2+4d)p^{-2}.
\end{gathered}
\tag{7}
\]
For the fourth inequality, the exact difference is
\[
q_p-p^{-2}=\frac{2-p\rho(p)}{p^2(p^2-2)},
\]
whose modulus is at most \(4p^{-4}+2dp^{-3}\leq(2+2d)p^{-3}\).
The fifth follows by adding \(|a_p-1|p^{-2}\leq2dp^{-5}\).
For the last inequality, the bound before collecting powers is
\(2dp^{-3}+2p^{-2}+4dp^{-5}\), which is at most the stated bound.

Set \(z=p^{-s}\). The local factor of \(H_f\) is exactly
\[
L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})
 \left[a_p+u_pz+(q_p-a_pp^{-2})z^2
                    -u_pp^{-2}z^3-q_pp^{-2}z^4\right].
\]
Since \(|z|=p^{-\sigma}\leq p^{5/8}\), (7) implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
|L_p(s)-1|\leq{}& (2+4d)p^{-2}+4dp^{-19/8}
 +(2+4d)p^{-7/4}\\
&+4dp^{-25/8}+(d+2)p^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)p^{-3/2}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
The prime sum of these bounds is at most
\[
(6+17d)\sum_{n=2}^\infty n^{-3/2}
\leq(6+17d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\,du
=2(6+17d).
\]
Thus the product over \(p\notin\mathcal B\) has modulus at most
\(\exp(2(6+17d))\). The remaining product has exactly
\(|\mathcal B|\) factors. Before multiplication each such factor is
bounded by the following finite number:
\[
U_p=(1-2p^{-2})(1+p^{-3/4})
       \left(|a_p|+|u_p|p^{5/8}+|q_p|p^{5/4}\right).
\]
After multiplication their modulus is at most
\(\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p\), with the empty product equal to one.
Therefore
\[
|H_f(s)|\leq M_H,
\qquad
M_H=\exp(2(6+17d))\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}U_p,
\quad -5/8\leq\Re s\leq2.
\tag{9}
\]
Combining (1), (4), (5), and (9), define
\[
C_D=M_H\max\{C_{1/4},Q3^{9/8}C_{3/4}\}
                    2^{1/4}C_{3/4}.
\]
We then have the explicit growth estimate
\[
|D_f(\sigma+it)|\leq C_D|t|^{13/8}
\quad(-5/8\leq\sigma\leq2,\ |t|\geq2),
\tag{10}
\]
where the exponent is \(11/8+1/4=13/8\).

## 3. Mellin representation and contour displacement

The elementary kernel identity needed here is, for \(v>0\),
\[
\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}
             \frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\,dz
=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\geq1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]
For completeness, close a finite rectangle to the left when \(v\geq1\),
and to the right when \(v<1\). On a fixed horizontal segment at height
\(T\), the denominator has modulus at least \(T^3\), so those integrals
tend to zero as \(T\) tends to infinity. A new left edge
\(\Re z=-N-1/2\), \(N\geq3\), has normalized integral in modulus at most
\[
\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi}
\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}
       \frac{dt}{((N-3/2)^2+t^2)^{3/2}}
=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2},
\]
because each of
\(|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|\) is at least
\(\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\Im z)^2}\). This tends to zero also at \(v=1\).
A new right edge \(\Re z=N\) has normalized integral at most
\(2v^N/(\pi N^2)\), which tends to zero for \(v<1\). The left-hand residues
are \(1,-2v^{-1},v^{-2}\), respectively, at \(0,-1,-2\). Their sum is
the first expression in (11), including its value zero at \(v=1\).

Apply (11) with \(v=H/h\), multiply by \(H^2W_f(h)/h\), and sum over
positive integers \(h\). P5 gives
\(A_2:=\sum_{h=1}^\infty|W_f(h)|h^{-2}<\infty\).
On putting \(s=z+1\), the sum of absolute values of the integrands on
\(\Re s=2\) is bounded by
\[
\frac{2H^3 A_2}{|(s-1)s(s+1)|}.
\]
Its integral over the entire vertical line is finite: for \(|\Im s|\geq1\)
it is at most \(2H^3A_2|\Im s|^{-3}\), and on the remaining compact
segment the denominator does not vanish. Absolute convergence therefore
justifies the exchange of the infinite sum and integral. It gives
\[
\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\,ds,
\qquad
G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
\tag{12}
\]
The equality holds for all real \(H\geq1\); an integer endpoint has
weight zero in both (11) and the definition of \(\Theta_f\).

Shift the contour to \(\Re s=-5/8\). The only possible poles of
\(D_f\) in the intervening strip are at \(1\) and \(-1/2\), from
\(\zeta(s)\) and \(\zeta(2s+2)\), respectively. This follows from
(1), the analyticity of \(H_f\) supplied by P5, and the zeta properties
checked in Section 1. The kernel additionally has a pole at zero; its
pole at \(-1\) lies outside the strip.

Here are explicit bounds justifying the displacement. At heights
\(\pm T\), \(T\geq2\), each denominator factor in (12) has modulus at
least \(T\), while \(H^{\sigma+1}\leq H^3\) because \(H\geq1\).
Thus (10) gives the bound
\[
|G_H(\sigma\pm iT)|\leq2C_DH^3T^{13/8-3}
                         =2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}.
\]
Each horizontal segment has length \(2+5/8=21/8\). After integration
over both segments, the bound is at most
\[
\frac{21}{2}C_DH^3T^{-11/8},
\]
which tends to zero for each fixed \(H\). This limit is taken before
asserting the uniform bound for the resulting left vertical integral.

For that vertical line define the finite constant
\[
M_0=\max_{|t|\leq2}|D_f(-5/8+it)|.
\]
It is finite because the line contains no poles. Its denominator in
(12) satisfies, for all real \(t\),
\[
|(s-1)s(s+1)|\geq\frac{13}{8}\frac58\frac38=\frac{195}{512}.
\]
The compact part of the line has length four; before integration its
integrand is bounded by
\((1024/195)M_0H^{3/8}\), so after integration it contributes at most
\((4096/195)M_0H^{3/8}\) to the absolute integral. On either infinite
tail, (10) gives
\[
|G_H(-5/8+it)|\leq2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}
\qquad(|t|\geq2).
\]
After integration over both tails the bound is
\[
4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\,dt
=\frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}.
\]
In particular, the left integral is absolutely convergent, and
\[
\left|\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{-5/8-i\infty}^{-5/8+i\infty}
                                      G_H(s)\,ds\right|
\leq C_*H^{3/8},
\tag{13}
\]
where the finite constant depending only on \(f\) can be taken to be
\[
C_* =\frac1{2\pi}
       \left(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+
                         \frac{32}{3}C_D2^{-3/8}\right).
\tag{14}
\]
The residue theorem on the finite rectangles, followed by the limits
just justified, now gives (12) as the sum of the three residues and the
left integral.

## 4. Residues and the two estimates

Write the Laurent expansion at one as
\[
D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+(s-1)J_f(s),
\]
Here P5 identifies \(R_f=P_f(1)\), and the definition in the statement
gives \(B_f=L_f-3R_f/2\). Here \(J_f\) is analytic on a fixed disk
about one. On a smaller closed disk choose a finite constant \(A_f\)
with \(|J_f(s)|\leq A_f\); the local remainder is therefore bounded
by \(A_f|s-1|\). No such
local remainder is summed or integrated in the argument.

Set \(q(s)=2/[s(s+1)]\). Direct differentiation gives
\(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). Hence the residue of
\(q(s)D_f(s)H^{s+1}/(s-1)\) at one is exactly
\[
H^2\left(L_f+R_f\log H-\frac32R_f\right)
=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
\tag{15}
\]
At zero, P5 gives \(D_f(0)=-1/(2\zeta(2))=-c/2\), and consequently
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=0}G_H(s)
=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
\tag{16}
\]
At \(-1/2\), the denominator \((s-1)s(s+1)\) equals \(3/8\).
Using exactly the definition of \(K_f\) in the statement, we obtain
\[
\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}G_H(s)
=\frac{16}{3}H^{1/2}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-K_fH^{1/2}.
\tag{17}
\]
This definition agrees with the one in P5: the simple pole of
\(\zeta(2s+2)\) has residue \(1/2\), so (1) gives
\[
-\frac{16}{3}\mathop{\rm Res}_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)
=-\frac83\zeta(-1/2)H_f(-1/2).
\]

Let \(E_f(H)\) denote the normalized left vertical integral in (13).
Equations (12)–(17) establish the exact formula
\[
\Theta_f(H)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}+E_f(H),
\qquad |E_f(H)|\leq C_*H^{3/8}
\tag{18}
\]
for every real \(H\geq1\). Thus no loss depending on whether \(H\) is
an integer is present. Choose \(C(f)=1+C_*\), which is strictly positive.
The first asserted inequality follows from (18). Substituting (18) into
the definition of \(F_f\) gives the exact identity
\[
F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-\frac{E_f(H)}{H^2}.
\]
Therefore
\[
|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}|
\leq C_*H^{3/8-2}=C_*H^{-13/8}
\leq C(f)H^{-13/8},
\]
which proves the second assertion with the same constant.

## 5. The integral identity

Fix real \(x\geq2\) and \(2\leq Z\leq Y\leq x\), and put
\(r_+=\max(r,0)\). Throughout \(Z\leq t\leq Y\), every nonzero
term of the integrand has \(h\leq x/Z\). Thus only
\(\lfloor x/Z\rfloor\) integers can occur, and we may write the
finite sum identity
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}W_f(h)
                                  2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt.
\tag{19}
\]
For each such positive integer \(h\), the function
\((x-ht)_+^2\) is continuously differentiable, including at
\(t=x/h\), and its derivative is \(-2h(x-ht)_+\). Therefore its
integral is exactly
\[
2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\,dt
=\frac{(x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2}{h}.
\tag{20}
\]
Multiplying out the definition of \(\Theta_f\) gives
\[
Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hZ)_+^2,
\]
and
\[
Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)
=\sum_{h=1}^{\lfloor x/Z\rfloor}\frac{W_f(h)}h(x-hY)_+^2.
\]
In the second equality, terms with \(h>x/Y\) vanish, so the indicated
extension of its finite summation range changes its value by exactly
zero. Subtract these two equalities and use (19)–(20). The result is
\[
2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\leq h\leq x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt
=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\]
This is exact throughout the requested range, and has no error term.

Exact symbolic checks in Python/SymPy verified the local-factor
expansion, the kernel coefficient at \(-1/2\), the kernel residue at
zero, and \(q(1)=1\), \(q'(1)=-3/2\). No numerical sanity check was
used. No excluded source or previous-run write-up was consulted, and no
objections file was supplied for this attempt.
=========== P7 proof
# Proof of P7

We use the supplied propositions P2–P6 as black boxes. No external literature
is used. Write
\[
c=\zeta(2)^{-1},\qquad
a=4d-1,\qquad \theta=\frac{2d}{a},\qquad
\eta=\min\left\{\frac15,\frac1a\right\}.
\]
Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\eta/2\), and set
\(\delta=\varepsilon/2\). Every constant below is independent of \(x,y\);
constants denoted by \(C_f\) depend only on \(f\), and those denoted by
\(C_{f,\varepsilon}\) depend only on \(f,\varepsilon\). Constants may be
enlarged from one occurrence to the next.

## Polynomial bounds and identification of the density

The assumptions in problem.md are \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\), \(d\ge1\),
\(f(t)\ge2\), and \(f'(t)\ge1\) for every real \(t\ge1\).
The leading coefficient of \(f\) is positive, because \(f(t)\ge2\) on
this half-line. The functions \(f(t)/t^d\) and
\(f'(t)/t^{d-1}\) tend to positive limits as \(t\to\infty\).
Continuity on each bounded closed subinterval of \([1,\infty)\), and
the positivity assumptions, therefore give constants \(b_f,B_f^*>0\)
such that
\[
b_f t^d\le f(t)\le B_f^*t^d,
\qquad 0<f'(t)\le B_f^*t^{d-1}\quad(t\ge1).
\tag{1}
\]
Here \(B_f^*\) is just a bound, distinct from the constant \(B_f\)
in the statement. In particular,
\[
\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le \frac{B_f^*}{b_f k}\quad(k\ge1),
\qquad y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\quad\text{if }f(y)\le x.
\tag{2}
\]

The coefficient of \(\log(Y/Z)\) in P4 is the \(R_f\) in the
statement. Indeed, P5 gives
\[
D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s),\qquad
P_f(1)=\sum_{r\ge1}\frac{\lambda(r)\rho(r)}r.
\]
Its asserted convergence makes \(P_f\) holomorphic near \(1\), so the
residue at \(1\) is \(P_f(1)\), which is exactly the coefficient in
P4. All the definitions of \(W_f,\Theta_f,F_f,R_f,B_f,K_f\) in P6
are those in P7. Thus P6 applies with these definitions and yields a
constant \(C_f\) such that
\[
\left|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}\right|\le C_fH^{-13/8}
\quad(H\ge1).
\tag{3}
\]
Since \(H^{-13/8}\le H^{-3/2}\) for \(H\ge1\), enlarging the
constant to include \(|K_f|\) gives
\[
|F_f(H)|\le C_fH^{-3/2}\quad(H\ge1).
\tag{4}
\]

## Reduction on an interval of moduli

For the moment let \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
\(2\le Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\).
Put
\[
\begin{split}
M(x;z,y)&=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)
  \sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}(x-hf(k))\mathfrak S(hf(k)),\\
I(x;Z,Y)&=\int_Z^Y
  \sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\,dt,\\
A(x,Z,R)&=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
       +R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x).
\end{split}
\tag{5}
\]
All discrete variables in these expressions are positive integers.

We first record the correlation error with both summation lengths.
For a fixed integer \(k\) with \(z<k\le y\), there are
\(N_k=\lfloor x/f(k)\rfloor\le x/f(k)\) choices of \(h\).
For each choice, \(m=hf(k)\) is an integer satisfying
\(1\le m\le x\): integrality follows from \(f\in\mathbb Z[t]\),
and the upper bound follows from the restriction on \(h\).
Consequently P3 with exponent \(\delta\) bounds each unweighted
correlation error by \(C_\delta x^{4/5+\delta}\). After multiplication
by the positive weight \(f'(k)\) and summation over these \(N_k\)
values, the error is at most
\[
C_\delta f'(k)N_kx^{4/5+\delta}
\le C_\delta x^{9/5+\delta}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}.
\tag{6}
\]
There are \(\lfloor y\rfloor-\lfloor z\rfloor\le\lfloor y\rfloor
\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\) possible values of \(k\). Use (2) to sum (6):
\[
\begin{split}
|S_f(x;z,y)-M(x;z,y)|
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}
       \sum_{1\le k\le y}\frac1k\\
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}(1+\log y)\\
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x).
\end{split}
\tag{7}
\]
The last inequality uses \(y\le b_f^{-1/d}x^{1/d}\), with its
constant depending only on \(f\).

P4, applied with precisely the ranges preceding (5), gives the two
errors
\[
|M(x;z,y)-I(x;Z,Y)|\le C_fx^2A(x,Z,R),
\qquad
|T_f(z,y)-R_f\log(Y/Z)|\le C_fA(x,Z,R).
\tag{8}
\]
The hypotheses needed here are exactly \(x\ge2\), \(1\le z\le y\),
\(Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x\), and \(2\le R\le x\), together
with the polynomial assumptions already checked. No extra arithmetic
assumption on \(f\) is being introduced.

Use P2 with exponent \(\delta\), substitute (7) and (8), and retain
the factors \(2\) and \(x^2\) multiplying the errors of \(S_f\) and
\(T_f\). This gives
\[
\begin{split}
\big|V_f(x;z,y)-[cx(Y-Z)+2I(x;Z,Y)-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)]\big|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}
  +xY^{1-1/d}\\
 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
\end{split}
\tag{9}
\]
More explicitly, the two substitutions in the \(S_f\) term contribute
at most \(2C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)
+2C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\), and the substitution in the \(T_f\) term
contributes at most \(C_fx^2A(x,Z,R)\). These are the last two
terms on the right of (9), after enlarging its constant.

The integral identity in P6 is applicable because \(2\le Z\le Y\le x\).
It is exact:
\[
2I(x;Z,Y)=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\tag{10}
\]
From the definition of \(F_f\), direct subtraction gives the exact
identity
\[
\begin{split}
x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)
={}&-x^2R_f\log(Y/Z)+cx(Y-Z)\\
 &+Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
\end{split}
\tag{11}
\]
In particular the \(B_f\) terms cancel. Combining (9)–(11) proves
\[
\begin{split}
\big|V_f(x;z,y)-x^2\big(F_f(x/Y)-F_f(x/Z)\big)\big|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[&x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}\\
 &+x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big].
\end{split}
\tag{12}
\]

## The cutoff and its error budget

Take
\[
Z=x^\theta=x^{2d/a},\qquad R=Z^{1/d}=x^{2/a}.
\tag{13}
\]
We have \(0<\theta<1\) and \(0<2/a<1\) for every integer
\(d\ge1\). Choose \(x_0=x_0(f,\varepsilon)\ge2\) large enough
that \(Z\ge\max\{2,f(1)\}\) and \(R\ge2\) whenever
\(x\ge x_0\). Then \(Z\le x\) and \(R\le x\).
Since \(f'(t)\ge1\) for \(t\ge1\), the polynomial is strictly
increasing there, continuous, and unbounded. Hence there is a unique
real \(z\ge1\) with \(f(z)=Z\). If \(Y\ge Z\), strict
monotonicity gives \(z\le y\), so every hypothesis used for (12)
holds for the choices (13).

The powers in \(A\) are
\[
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}=x^{-2/a}x^{1/a}=x^{-1/a},
\qquad R^{-1/2}=x^{-1/a}.
\]
As \(R\le x\), the two terms of \(A\), separately, satisfy
\[
\begin{split}
Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log(2R))^2
 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^2,\\
R^{-1/2}(\log(2R))^2\log(2x)
 &\le x^{-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
\end{split}
\]
It follows that
\[
x^2A(x,Z,R)\le Cx^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3.
\tag{14}
\]

The initial-modulus estimate in P2, with exponent \(\delta\), applies
to this \(z\), since \(z\ge1\) and \(f(z)=Z\le x\). It gives
\[
0\le V_f(x,z)
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}
=C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-1/a+\delta},
\tag{15}
\]
where the exponent calculation is
\[
1+\theta(2-1/d)=1+\frac{4d-2}{a}=2-\frac1a.
\tag{16}
\]
The other boundary contribution is controlled by (4), because \(x/Z\ge1\):
\[
x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}
=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}.
\tag{17}
\]
For all \(d\ge1\),
\[
\left(2-\frac1a\right)-\left(\frac12+\frac{3d}{a}\right)
=\frac{6d-5}{2a}>0.
\tag{18}
\]
Thus (17) is at most \(C_fx^{2-1/a}\).

Here is the complete comparison of the errors in (12), (15), and
(17) with the target exponent. For \(x\ge2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
x^{3/2+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\eta\le1/5\text{ and }\delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
xY^{1-1/d}&\le x^{2-1/d}\le x^{2-\eta},
&&\text{since }Y\le x,\ 1-1/d\ge0,\ 1/d\ge\eta,\\
x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)&\le
 C_\varepsilon x^{9/5+\varepsilon}
 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\log(2x)\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/5,\\
x^{2-1/a}(\log(2x))^3&\le
 C_\varepsilon x^{2-1/a+\varepsilon/2}
 \le C_\varepsilon x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }(\log(2x))^3\le C_\varepsilon x^{\varepsilon/2},\ \eta\le1/a,\\
x^{2-1/a+\delta}&\le x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon},
&&\text{since }\eta\le1/a,\ \delta=\varepsilon/2,\\
x^{1/2+3d/a}&\le x^{2-1/a}\le x^{2-\eta},
&&\text{by (18) and }\eta\le1/a.
\end{aligned}
\tag{19}
\]
The logarithm bounds used here follow, for any fixed positive power
\(u\), from boundedness of \((\log(2x))^j/x^u\) on \([2,\infty)\)
for \(j=1,3\). Their constants depend only on \(\varepsilon\).

For \(Y\ge Z\), the defining sums split exactly as
\[
V_f(x,y)=V_f(x,z)+V_f(x;z,y).
\]
Subtracting \(x^2F_f(x/Y)\), using (12), and then applying
(14)–(19) gives
\[
\begin{split}
|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|
&\le V_f(x,z)+x^2|F_f(x/Z)|\\
&\quad+C_{f,\varepsilon}\big[x^{3/2+\delta}+xY^{1-1/d}
       +x^{9/5+\delta}\log(2x)+x^2A(x,Z,R)\big]\\
&\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.
\end{split}
\tag{20}
\]

## Moduli below the cutoff

Suppose instead that \(Y<Z=x^\theta\). Apply the initial-modulus
bound in P2 directly with its argument \(z\) equal to \(y\).
Its hypotheses hold because \(y\ge1\) and \(f(y)=Y\le x\).
The exponent \(2-1/d\) is positive, so (16) gives
\[
0\le V_f(x,y)
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Y^{2-1/d}
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{1+\delta}Z^{2-1/d}
=C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-1/a+\delta}.
\tag{21}
\]
Also \(x/Y\ge1\), so (4) and (18) imply
\[
x^2|F_f(x/Y)|
\le C_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}
\le C_fx^{1/2}Z^{3/2}
=C_fx^{1/2+3d/a}
\le C_fx^{2-1/a}.
\tag{22}
\]
The triangle inequality, (21), (22), and \(\eta\le1/a\) therefore
give
\[
|V_f(x,y)-x^2F_f(x/Y)|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}.
\tag{23}
\]
Together, (20) and (23) prove the first assertion uniformly for all
the required \(x,y\).

## The power main term

For every \(Y\le x\), apply (3) with \(H=x/Y\ge1\) and multiply
by \(x^2\). Tracking the powers gives
\[
\begin{split}
\left|x^2F_f(x/Y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\right|
&\le C_fx^2(x/Y)^{-13/8}\\
&=C_fx^{3/8}Y^{13/8},
\end{split}
\tag{24}
\]
where \(x^2(x/Y)^{-3/2}=x^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\) identifies the main term.
Combining (24) with the first assertion proves
\[
\left|V_f(x,y)-K_fx^{1/2}Y^{3/2}\right|
\le C_{f,\varepsilon}
\left[x^{3/8}Y^{13/8}+x^{2-\eta+\varepsilon}\right].
\]
Enlarge one constant to cover both asserted inequalities. The choices
of \(x_0\) and all constants made above depend only on \(f\) and
\(\varepsilon\), as required. No numerical sanity checks were used
in this proof.

\chapter{Correlations of squarefree numbers}\label{ch:correlations}

The off-diagonal term $S_f$ is a weighted sum of the correlations $C_x(m)$ of \eqref{eq:Cx}. We need an asymptotic formula for $C_x(m)$ that is uniform in the whole range $1\le m\le x$, including differences $m$ close to $x$, where the number $x-m$ of available pairs is small. Counts of pairs of squarefree numbers with a given difference have a long history (see for example \cite{mirsky1949}, and the discussion of the related binary additive problem in \cite[\S1]{bgpvw1998}). The archived proof gives a self-contained elementary argument with an explicit absolute constant. The archived plan anticipated a circle-method argument based on \cite{bgpvw1998}, but the proof does not need it. (Archived source: proposition P3.)

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:corr}
There is an absolute constant $K_{\mathrm c}$ such that for all real $x\ge2$ and all integers $1\le m\le x$,
\[
\bigl|C_x(m)-(x-m)\Sing(m)\bigr|\le K_{\mathrm c}\,x^{4/5}.
\]
One may take $K_{\mathrm c}=67+2D_{1/10}$, with $D_{1/10}$ as in \cref{lem:divisor}. In particular, for every $\eps>0$ the bound $C(\eps)x^{4/5+\eps}$ holds, which is the form recorded in the archived plan.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Put $L=x-m\ge0$ and $H=\lfloor x^{2/5}\rfloor$, so that $\frac12x^{2/5}\le H\le x^{2/5}$ and $H\ge1$. All bounds below hold for every real $L\ge0$, including $L<1$, when $C_x(m)=0$.

\emph{Truncation.} For $k\ge1$ split \eqref{eq:mu2} as $\mu^2(k)=T_H(k)+R_H(k)$, where
\[
T_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e\le H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e),\qquad R_H(k)=\sum_{\substack{e>H\\e^2\mid k}}\mu(e).
\]
Then $|T_H(k)|\le\tau(k)$ and $|R_H(k)|\le\#\{e>H:e^2\mid k\}$. Each of the sets $\{n:1\le n\le L\}$ and $\{n+m:1\le n\le L\}$ consists of integers in $[1,x]$, because $m+L=x$. Each contains at most $x/e^2$ multiples of $e^2$. Therefore, by \cref{lem:sums}(a),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:RH-sum}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n)|\le\sum_{e>H}\frac x{e^2}\le\frac xH,\qquad\sum_{1\le n\le L}|R_H(n+m)|\le\frac xH.
\end{equation}
The exact identity
\[
\mu^2(n)\mu^2(n+m)-T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=R_H(n)\mu^2(n+m)+T_H(n)R_H(n+m)
\]
together with $0\le\mu^2\le1$ and $|T_H(n)|\le\tau(n)\le D_{1/10}x^{1/10}$ (\cref{lem:divisor}) bounds each summand by $|R_H(n)|+D_{1/10}x^{1/10}|R_H(n+m)|$. Summing with \eqref{eq:RH-sum},
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-trunc}
\Bigl|C_x(m)-\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)\Bigr|\le(1+D_{1/10}x^{1/10})\frac xH\le2x^{3/5}+2D_{1/10}x^{7/10}.
\end{equation}

\emph{Counting the truncated congruences.} Let $e_1,e_2\le H$ and $g=(e_1,e_2)$. The congruences $n\equiv0\bmod e_1^2$ and $n\equiv-m\bmod e_2^2$ are soluble exactly when $g^2\mid m$. Necessity follows by reducing modulo $g^2$. For sufficiency write $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ with $(a,b)=1$ and $n=e_1^2u$; the second congruence becomes $a^2u\equiv-m/g^2\bmod b^2$, which determines $u$ modulo $b^2$. Hence the solutions form one residue class modulo $e_1^2e_2^2/g^2$. For any residue class modulo $h$ with representative $r$, the number of its members in $[1,L]$ is $\lfloor(L-r)/h\rfloor-\lfloor-r/h\rfloor=L/h+\theta$ with $|\theta|\le1$. Expanding both truncated sums therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-AH}
\sum_{1\le n\le L}T_H(n)T_H(n+m)=L\,\mathcal A_H(m)+E_H,\qquad|E_H|\le H^2\le x^{4/5},
\end{equation}
where
\[
\mathcal A_H(m)=\sum_{\substack{e_1,e_2\le H\\(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m}}\frac{\mu(e_1)\mu(e_2)(e_1,e_2)^2}{e_1^2e_2^2}.
\]

\emph{Completing the series.} Let $\mathcal A(m)$ denote the same sum over all $e_1,e_2\ge1$. Writing $e_1=ga$, $e_2=gb$ and dropping the coprimality of $a,b$ shows absolute convergence:
$\sum_{e_1,e_2}(e_1,e_2)^2/(e_1e_2)^2\le\sum_gg^{-2}\sum_aa^{-2}\sum_bb^{-2}\le8$. For the tail with $e_1>H$, the same substitution gives the bound $\sum_gg^{-2}\bigl(\sum_{a>H/g}a^{-2}\bigr)\bigl(\sum_bb^{-2}\bigr)$. For $g\le H$ the summand is at most $g^{-2}(2g/H)\cdot2=4/(gH)$ by \cref{lem:sums}(a), and summing over $g\le H$ gives at most $4(1+\log H)/H$. For $g>H$ the summand is at most $4/g^2$, and these sum to at most $4/H$. By symmetry the tail with $e_2>H$ has the same bound, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corr-tail}
|\mathcal A(m)-\mathcal A_H(m)|\le\frac{8(2+\log H)}H,
\end{equation}
uniformly in $m$, because the condition $(e_1,e_2)^2\mid m$ was dropped.

\emph{The Euler product.} By absolute convergence, $\mathcal A(m)$ factors over primes, the argument of \cref{lem:euler} applying verbatim to the double sum. Only the exponents $0$ and $1$ occur in $e_1,e_2$. At a prime $p$ the four choices contribute $1$, $-p^{-2}$, $-p^{-2}$, and $p^{-2}\one_{p^2\mid m}$, so by \eqref{eq:sing}
\[
\mathcal A(m)=\prod_p\Bigl(1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\one_{p^2\mid m}}{p^2}\Bigr)=\Sing(m).
\]

\emph{Conclusion.} Since $0\le L\le x$, $H\ge\frac12x^{2/5}$ and $\log H\le\frac25\log x\le2x^{1/5}$ (\cref{lem:sums}(d)), \eqref{eq:corr-tail} gives
\[
L\,|\mathcal A_H(m)-\Sing(m)|\le16x^{3/5}\bigl(2+\tfrac25\log x\bigr)\le32x^{3/5}+32x^{4/5}\le64x^{4/5}.
\]
Combining with \eqref{eq:corr-trunc} and \eqref{eq:corr-AH} gives $|C_x(m)-L\Sing(m)|\le(2+2D_{1/10}+1+64)x^{4/5}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The constant $D_{1/10}$ is astronomically large, but only its existence matters. For the application in \cref{ch:assembly} only the exponent $4/5$ is relevant: summing the error over the roughly $x\log x$ weighted pairs $(h,k)$ costs $x^{9/5+\eps}$, and this caps the saving in \cref{thm:main} at $\eta_d\le1/5$.
\end{remark}
\chapter{Averaging over polynomial moduli}\label{ch:averaging}

After \cref{ch:variance,ch:correlations} the variance is expressed through two sums over $k$: the density term $T_f(z,y)$ and the main part of the off-diagonal term,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Mf}
M_f(x;z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)\sum_{1\le h\le x/f(k)}\bigl(x-hf(k)\bigr)\Sing\bigl(hf(k)\bigr).
\end{equation}
Both involve arithmetic functions of $f(k)$. Expanding them over $r$ with the coefficients $\lambda(r)$ of \cref{ch:densities} makes the dependence on $k$ periodic modulo $r$. Partial summation then replaces the sum over $k$ by an integral in the variable $t=f(k)$, with $f'(k)$ acting as the Jacobian. This is the role of the weight $f'(k)$. (Archived source: proposition P4, a crux of the plan.)

\section{The averaged singular series}

For $h\ge1$ and a prime $p$ put
\[
\delta_p(h)=\frac1{p^2}\#\{a\bmod p^2:\ p^2\mid hf(a)\}.
\]
If $j=\max\{2-v_p(h),0\}$, then $p^2\mid hf(a)$ is equivalent to $p^j\mid f(a)$. Counting lifts from residues modulo $p^j$ to residues modulo $p^2$ gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:deltap}
\delta_p(h)=\frac{\rho(p^{j})}{p^{j}}\in[0,1],\qquad\text{so}\qquad
1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\end{equation}
where $w_p(h)$ is the local factor in \eqref{eq:W-intro}. Comparing with the second form of \eqref{eq:sing}, $W_f(h)=\prod_pw_p(h)$ is what one obtains by replacing the indicator $\one_{p^2\mid hf(k)}$ in $\Sing(hf(k))$ by its average $\delta_p(h)$ over $k$. \Cref{lem:W-ident} below makes this precise.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-basic}
For every $h\ge1$ and prime $p$, $1-2p^{-2}\le w_p(h)\le1-p^{-2}$. Hence the product $W_f(h)$ converges absolutely, uniformly in $h$, and $0<W_f(h)\le1$. The series
\[
\widetilde R_f=\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\frac{\rho(r)}r
\]
converges absolutely and $0\le\widetilde R_f\le c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The bounds for $w_p$ follow from $\delta_p(h)\in[0,1]$, so $|w_p(h)-1|\le2p^{-2}$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. The factors are positive, so $W_f(h)>0$, and they are at most one. Finally $0\le\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$.
\end{proof}

For $r,h\ge1$ define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta}
\beta_r(h)=\frac1r\sum_{a=1}^r\frac{c_r(hf(a))}{\varphi(r)},
\end{equation}
the mean value of the $r$-periodic sequence
\[
k\longmapsto\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
Note $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ by \cref{lem:ramanujan}(b).

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:W-ident}
For every $h\ge1$, $\sum_{r\ge1}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=W_f(h)$, the series converging absolutely and uniformly in $h$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Absolute and uniform convergence follow from $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$ and $\sum_r\lambda(r)=c$. If $(r,s)=1$, the Chinese remainder theorem identifies $a\bmod rs$ with pairs $(a\bmod r,\ a\bmod s)$. Moreover $c_{rs}=c_rc_s$, $c_r(hf(a))$ depends only on $a\bmod r$, and $\varphi(rs)=\varphi(r)\varphi(s)$. Hence $\beta_{rs}(h)=\beta_r(h)\beta_s(h)$. Thus $\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)$ is $c^2$ times a multiplicative function supported on cube-free $r$, and \cref{lem:euler} gives
\[
\sum_r\lambda(r)\beta_r(h)=c^2\prod_p\Bigl(1+\frac{(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)
\]
by \eqref{eq:lambda-p}. The average defining $\beta_p(h)$ may equally be taken over $a\bmod p^2$, since its summand has period $p$. Therefore, by \eqref{eq:cp-sum},
\[
(p-1)\beta_p(h)+(p^2-p)\beta_{p^2}(h)=\frac1{p^2}\sum_{a\bmod p^2}\bigl(c_p+c_{p^2}\bigr)(hf(a))=p^2\delta_p(h)-1.
\]
Distributing $c^2=\prod_p(1-p^{-2})^2$ over the primes, the local factor becomes
\[
\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\Bigl(1+\frac{p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{(p^2-1)^2}\Bigr)=\frac{(p^2-1)^2+p^2\delta_p(h)-1}{p^4}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\delta_p(h)}{p^2}=w_p(h),
\]
by \eqref{eq:deltap}. No restriction on $f$ modulo $p$ has been used.
\end{proof}

\section{A partial summation lemma}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:periodic}
Let $b$ be a periodic sequence with integer period $r\ge1$, $|b(k)|\le1$, and mean $m_b=r^{-1}\sum_{a=1}^rb(a)$. Let $1\le u\le v$ be real and let $F$ be continuously differentiable on $[u,v]$. Then
\[
\Bigl|\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t\Bigr|\le4r\Bigl(|F(v)|+\int_u^v|F'(t)|\dd t\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $P(t)=\sum_{k\le t}b(k)-m_bt$. Writing $t=qr+s$ with $q=\lfloor t/r\rfloor$ and $0\le s<r$, the $q$ complete periods cancel, the remaining at most $r$ terms have modulus at most $1$, and $|m_bs|\le r$; so $|P(t)|\le2r$. Hence $D_u(t)=\sum_{u<k\le t}b(k)-m_b(t-u)=P(t)-P(u)$ satisfies $|D_u(t)|\le4r$ and $D_u(u)=0$. Riemann--Stieltjes integration by parts gives the identity
\[
\sum_{u<k\le v}b(k)F(k)-m_b\int_u^vF(t)\dd t=\int_u^vF(t)\dd D_u(t)=F(v)D_u(v)-\int_u^vF'(t)D_u(t)\dd t,
\]
from which the bound follows.
\end{proof}

With $F=w=f'/f$ on $[z,y]$, \cref{lem:poly}(b) gives $|w(y)|\le U/y\le U/z$ and $\int_z^y|w'|\le V/z$. Since $\int_z^yw=\log(Y/Z)$, we obtain for every $r$-periodic $b$ as in \cref{lem:periodic} and $1\le z\le y$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:periodic-w}
\Bigl|\sum_{z<k\le y}b(k)\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}-m_b\log\frac YZ\Bigr|\le\frac{4D_wr}z,\qquad D_w=U+V.
\end{equation}

\section{The averaging proposition}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:averaging}
There is $C(f)>0$ such that the following holds uniformly for real $x\ge2$, $1\le z\le y$ with $Z=f(z)\le Y=f(y)\le x$, and real $2\le R\le x$. With
\[
\mathcal A=\mathcal A(x,Z,R)=Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)
\]
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:If}
I_f(x;Z,Y)=\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t,
\end{equation}
we have
\begin{align}
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,\mathcal A,\label{eq:avg1}\\
\bigl|M_f(x;z,y)-I_f(x;Z,Y)\bigr|&\le C(f)\,x^2\mathcal A.\label{eq:avg2}
\end{align}
No condition on the discriminant, content or factorisation of $f$ is imposed.
\end{proposition}

Throughout the proof, $\mathcal T(R)$ and $\mathcal N(R)$ are as in \cref{prop:second-moment}(d), so that $\mathcal T(R)\le C_0R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2$ and $\mathcal N(R)\le C_0R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2$. If $z=y$ both assertions are trivial, so we assume $z<y$.

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg1}]
By \cref{prop:second-moment}(a) applied to $q=f(k)$,
\[
T_f(z,y)=\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\sum_{r\mid f(k)}\lambda(r).
\]
The part with $r>R$ is nonnegative and at most $\mathcal T(R)\sum_{z<k\le y}f'(k)/f(k)\le2U\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$ by \eqref{eq:sum-w}. For each $r\le R$, the sequence $b(k)=\one_{r\mid f(k)}$ has period $r$ and mean $\rho(r)/r$, so \eqref{eq:periodic-w} gives
\[
\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\one_{r\mid f(k)}=\frac{\rho(r)}r\log\frac YZ+e_r,\qquad|e_r|\le\frac{4D_wr}z.
\]
Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ produces an error at most $4D_w\mathcal N(R)/z$. Completing $\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r$ to $\widetilde R_f$ costs at most $\mathcal T(R)\log(Y/Z)\le\mathcal T(R)\log(2x)$, because $\rho(r)/r\le1$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$. Since $Z\le\kappa_2z^d$, we have $z^{-1}\le\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}$, and therefore
\[
\bigl|T_f(z,y)-\widetilde R_f\log(Y/Z)\bigr|\le C_0\Bigl(4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d}Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}

For the second assertion we first need a bound for the weight functions. Let $H_0=\lfloor x/Z\rfloor$. For $1\le h\le H_0$ define
\[
v_h=\min\{y,\,f^{-1}(x/h)\},\qquad F_h(t)=f'(t)\bigl(x-hf(t)\bigr)\quad(z\le t\le v_h),
\]
which is legitimate because $x/h\ge Z=f(z)$ (\cref{lem:poly}(a)). Then $z\le v_h\le(x/(\kappa_1h))^{1/d}$ and $0\le x-hf(t)\le x$ on $[z,v_h]$. Put
\[
K_2=\begin{cases}\kappa_2+\kappa_2^2/\kappa_1,&d=1,\\ \kappa_2+\kappa_2/(d-1)+\kappa_2^2/((2d-1)\kappa_1),&d\ge2.\end{cases}
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:weight-var}
For $1\le h\le H_0$, $\displaystyle|F_h(v_h)|+\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'(t)|\dd t\le K_2\,x\,v_h^{d-1}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have $|F_h(v_h)|\le\kappa_2xv_h^{d-1}$ and $|F_h'|\le|f''|(x-hf)+hf'^2$. For $d\ge2$,
\[
\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le\kappa_2x\int_z^{v_h}t^{d-2}\dd t+h\kappa_2^2\int_z^{v_h}t^{2d-2}\dd t\le\frac{\kappa_2}{d-1}xv_h^{d-1}+\frac{h\kappa_2^2}{2d-1}v_h^{2d-1},
\]
and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
\[
\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
\]
By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
\[
|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
\]
uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
\[
|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
\]
Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.

\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
\[
M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
\]
The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
\[
\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
\]
and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
\[
|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
\]

Combining the three estimates proves
\[
|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
\]
Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
\end{remark}
\chapter{The Dirichlet series of the averaged singular series}\label{ch:dirichlet}

The averaged singular series $W_f(h)$ is a product of local factors that depend only on whether $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. Its Dirichlet series therefore factors as $\zeta(s)$ times an Euler product, and a second factorisation exhibits a pole of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\frac12$. This pole, which is invisible in the region of absolute convergence, produces the main term of \cref{thm:main}. (Archived source: proposition P5, a crux of the plan.)

\section{Facts about the zeta function}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item For every integer $N\ge1$ and $\re w>0$, $w\ne1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-N}
\zeta(w)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}-w\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-w-1}\dd u.
\end{equation}
In $\re w>0$ the only pole of $\zeta$ is a simple pole at $w=1$ with residue $1$, and $\lim_{w\to1}\bigl(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\bigr)=\gamma_E$, Euler's constant.
\item Let $\mathcal B_2(u)=\{u\}^2-\{u\}+\frac16$. The formula
\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-B2}
\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}-\frac{w(w+1)}2\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u
\end{equation}
continues $\zeta$ meromorphically to $\re w>-1$, with the single pole at $w=1$. In particular $\zeta(0)=-\frac12$ and $-\frac14\le\zeta(-\frac12)\le-\frac16$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(a) For $\re w>1$ write $\sum_{n>N}n^{-w}=\int_N^\infty u^{-w}\dd\lfloor u\rfloor$, replace $\lfloor u\rfloor=u-\{u\}$, and integrate the second part by parts; the boundary term at $N$ vanishes because $\{N\}=0$. This gives \eqref{eq:zeta-N}. The integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $\re w>0$ because $0\le\{u\}<1$, which gives the continuation and the description of the pole. Subtracting $1/(w-1)$ and letting $w\to1$ gives $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N-\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-2}\dd u$. The integral lies in $[0,1/N]$, and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\gamma_E$ by its definition as $\lim(\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N)$.

(b) With $N=1$, \eqref{eq:zeta-N} becomes $\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12-w\int_1^\infty(\{u\}-\frac12)u^{-w-1}\dd u$. The function $\mathcal B_2$ is continuous, satisfies $|\mathcal B_2|\le\frac16$, and has derivative $2(\{u\}-\frac12)$ between integers. Integration by parts over $[1,T]$ for integers $T\ge2$ gives
\[
\int_1^T\Bigl(\{u\}-\frac12\Bigr)u^{-w-1}\dd u=\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}+\frac{w+1}2\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u,
\]
and letting $T\to\infty$ for $\re w>1$ yields \eqref{eq:zeta-B2}. The last integral and its $w$-derivatives are dominated on $\re w\ge\eta>-1$ by $(\log u)^mu^{-\eta-2}/6$, so the integral is holomorphic for $\re w>-1$. At $w=0$ the formula gives $-1+\frac12=-\frac12$. At $w=-\frac12$ it gives $\zeta(-\frac12)=-\frac5{24}+\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-3/2}\dd u$, and the integral has modulus at most $\frac16\cdot2=\frac13$.
\end{proof}

\section{The local factors}

For each prime $p$ put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd}
\alpha_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
\beta_p=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
\delta_p=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
\end{equation}
By \eqref{eq:W-intro}, $w_p(h)$ equals $\alpha_p$, $\alpha_p+\beta_p$ or $\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p$ according as $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. By \cref{lem:rho} (with $C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|\}$),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd-bounds}
1-\frac2{p^2}\le\alpha_p\le1,\quad0\le\beta_p\le\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}\le\frac{C_0}{p^3},\quad0\le\delta_p\le\frac1{p^2},\quad\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-\frac1{p^2}.
\end{equation}
Here $\beta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)$, $\delta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p)\le p$, and $\alpha_p\le1$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p^2$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:LM}
L_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s},\qquad
M_p(s)=\bigl(1-p^{-2s-2}\bigr)L_p(s),
\end{equation}
and $P_f(s)=\prod_pL_p(s)$, $H_f(s)=\prod_pM_p(s)$. In the notation of the archived proposition, $L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})B_p(s)$ with $B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p-a_p)p^{-s}+(c_p-b_p)p^{-2s}$, $a_p=1+\rho(p^2)/(p^2(p^2-2))$, $b_p=1+\rho(p)/(p(p^2-2))$, $c_p=1+1/(p^2-2)$. Expanding the product, with $z=p^{-s}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-expand}
M_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\bigl(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}\bigr)z^2-\beta_pp^{-2}z^3-\delta_pp^{-2}z^4,\qquad
\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}=-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6}.
\end{equation}
The cancellation of the terms $\pm p^{-2}$ in the coefficient of $z^2$ is what allows $H_f$ to converge beyond $\re s=-\frac12$.

\section{The factorisation}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Df}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item The series $D_f(s)=\sum_hW_f(h)h^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\re s>1$.
\item The products $P_f$ and $H_f$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, and define holomorphic functions, on $\re s>-\frac12$ and $\re s>-\frac34$ respectively. For every fixed $\sigma>-\frac34$ there is $C(f,\sigma)$ with $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le C(f,\sigma)$ for all real $t$.
\item For $\re s>1$, $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. The function $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ continues $D_f$ meromorphically to $\re s>-\frac34$, and its only possible poles there are simple poles at $s=1$ and $s=-\frac12$.
\item $R_f=\Res_{s=1}D_f(s)=P_f(1)$. Moreover $R_f=\widetilde R_f$, where $\widetilde R_f$ is the series of \cref{lem:W-basic}, and \eqref{eq:R-intro} holds. Moreover $B_f=(\gamma_E-\frac32)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and $R_f>0$.
\item $D_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}=-\frac c2$.
\item We have $\Res_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)=\frac12\zeta(-\frac12)H_f(-\frac12)$, and hence
\[
K_f=-\tfrac83\,\zeta(-\tfrac12)\,H_f(-\tfrac12).
\]
Moreover $H_f(-\frac12)>0$ and $K_f>0$, and $K_f$ is given by the absolutely convergent product \eqref{eq:K-intro}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(a) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $0<W_f(h)\le1$, so $\sum_h|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_hh^{-\re s}$.

(b) For $\re s\ge\sigma$, \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} gives $|L_p(s)-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}$. If $\sigma>-\frac12$ all exponents exceed one, so by \cref{lem:sums}(c) the sum over $p$ converges uniformly on $\re s\ge\sigma$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. For $M_p$, \eqref{eq:M-expand} and \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} give, for $\re s\ge\sigma$,
\[
|M_p(s)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}+\frac{C_0}{p^{3+\sigma}}+\Bigl(\frac{C_0}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}+\frac{C_0}{p^5}\Bigr)p^{-2\sigma}+\frac{C_0}{p^{5+3\sigma}}+\frac1{p^{4+4\sigma}}.
\]
For $\sigma>-\frac34$ the exponents $2$, $3+\sigma$, $3+2\sigma$, $4+2\sigma$, $5+2\sigma$, $5+3\sigma$ and $4+4\sigma$ all exceed one. Hence $\sum_p\sup_{\re s\ge\sigma}|M_p(s)-1|=:E_H(\sigma)<\infty$, and \cref{lem:products} gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, holomorphy, and $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(E_H(\sigma))$ for all $t$.

(c) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p>0$, and $u(h)=W_f(h)/W_f(1)$ is multiplicative with $u(p)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p)/\alpha_p$ and $u(p^e)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p)/\alpha_p$ for $e\ge2$. For $\re s>1$ and $z=p^{-s}$ its local series is
\[
1+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p}{\alpha_p}z+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p}{\alpha_p}\cdot\frac{z^2}{1-z}=\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\delta_pz^2}{\alpha_p(1-z)}=\frac{L_p(s)}{\alpha_p(1-p^{-s})}.
\]
Since $\sum_h|u(h)h^{-s}|<\infty$, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\sum_hu(h)h^{-s}=\prod_pL_p(s)\alpha_p^{-1}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. Multiplying by the convergent product $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p$ and using the Euler product of $\zeta$ gives $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)$; the limits of partial products multiply. For $\re s>-\frac12$ we have $\re(2s+2)>1$, so $\prod_p(1-p^{-2s-2})^{-1}=\zeta(2s+2)$ converges absolutely, and multiplying the products gives $P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. By \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(2s+2)$ are meromorphic for $\re s>-\frac34$, since then $\re s>-1$ and $\re(2s+2)>\frac12$. Their only poles there are at $s=1$ and at $2s+2=1$, both simple. Since $H_f$ is holomorphic, $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ is the required continuation.

(d) Since $P_f$ is holomorphic near $1$ and $\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1)$ by \cref{lem:zeta}(a), we have $D_f(s)=\frac{P_f(1)}{s-1}+\gamma_EP_f(1)+P_f'(1)+O(s-1)$. This gives $R_f=P_f(1)$ and the formula for $B_f$ from \eqref{eq:RBK}. Substituting \eqref{eq:abd},
\[
L_p(1)=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}p+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}
=\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\bigl(1+T_p\bigr),
\]
with $T_p=(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))/(p^2-1)^2\ge0$. By \cref{lem:rho}(d) and $p^2-1\ge\frac34p^2$, $T_p\le\frac{16C_0}9(p^{-3}+p^{-4})$, which is summable. Using \eqref{eq:c-euler}, $R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p(1+T_p)>0$, which is \eqref{eq:R-intro}. For the identification with $\widetilde R_f$, note that $\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=c^2v(r)$, where $v$ is the nonnegative multiplicative function supported on cube-free integers with
\[
v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad v(p^2)=\frac{\varphi(p^2)\rho(p^2)}{p^2(p^2-1)^2}=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2},
\]
using \cref{lem:rho}(a) for multiplicativity of $\rho$. Thus $1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p$. Since $\sum_rv(r)<\infty$ by \cref{lem:W-basic}, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\widetilde R_f=c^2\prod_p(1+T_p)=R_f$.

(e) $L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}$, so $P_f(0)=c$ by \eqref{eq:c-euler}. The identity $D_f=\zeta P_f$ persists on $\re s>-\frac12$ by (c), and both factors are regular at $0$; by \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $D_f(0)=\zeta(0)c=-c/2$.

(f) Near $s=-\frac12$, $\zeta(2s+2)=\frac{1/2}{s+1/2}+O(1)$, while $\zeta(s)$ and $H_f(s)$ are holomorphic. This gives the residue, and the formula for $K_f$ follows from \eqref{eq:RBK}. At $s=-\frac12$,
\[
M_p(-\tfrac12)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\Bigl(1+\frac1p-\frac{2+\rho(p)}{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p)}{p^{5/2}}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^{7/2}}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4}\Bigr),
\]
by direct substitution of \eqref{eq:abd}. This is positive because $\alpha_p>0$ and $\beta_p,\delta_p\ge0$. The deviations $|M_p(-\frac12)-1|$ are summable by (b), so \cref{lem:products}(c) gives $H_f(-\frac12)>0$, and \cref{lem:zeta}(b) gives $\zeta(-\frac12)<0$. The integral $I_f(x;Z,Y)$ of \cref{prop:averaging} turns out to be an exact combination of values of the smoothed partial sum

\section{Growth in a vertical strip}

We need one result from the literature. It is a consequence of the functional equation $\zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin(\pi s/2)$ \cite[Corollary~10.4]{montgomeryvaughan2007} and Stirling's formula.

\begin{quoted}[{\cite[Corollary~10.5]{montgomeryvaughan2007}}]\label{quoted:mv}
Suppose that $A>0$ is fixed. Then $|\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|$ uniformly for $|\sigma|\le A$ and $|t|\ge1$. Here $s=\sigma+it$ and $\tau=|t|+4$.
\end{quoted}

We use it with $A=2$, only for $-\frac58\le\sigma\le\frac14$ and $|t|\ge2$. Let $c_{\mathrm{MV}}$ be a constant for the upper inequality there, so that $|\zeta(s)|\le c_{\mathrm{MV}}(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|$. No conditional estimate for $\zeta$ is used. (The holomorphy of $\zeta$ in the strip away from $s=1$ is already contained in \cref{lem:zeta}(b).)

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta-growth}
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
\item Let $\delta\in\{\frac14,\frac34\}$ and $C_\delta=(\frac32)^{1-\delta}\bigl(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\bigr)+\frac4\delta$. Then $|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\le C_\delta|v|^{1-\delta}$ for $\delta\le\alpha\le6$ and $|v|\ge2$.
\item For $s=\sigma+it$ with $-\frac58\le\sigma\le2$ and $T=|t|\ge2$,
\[
|\zeta(s)|\le C_\zeta T^{11/8},\qquad|\zeta(2s+2)|\le C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4},\qquad C_\zeta=\max\{C_{1/4},\,3^{9/8}c_{\mathrm{MV}}C_{3/4}\}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(a) Let $V=|v|$ and use \eqref{eq:zeta-N} with $N=\lceil V\rceil$, so $V\le N\le\frac32V$. The finite sum has modulus at most $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-\delta}\le N^{1-\delta}/(1-\delta)\le(\frac32)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}/(1-\delta)$. Next, $|N^{1-s}/(s-1)|\le N^{1-\delta}/V\le(\frac32)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}$. Finally $|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\dd u|\le|s|N^{-\alpha}/\alpha\le(V+6)V^{-\delta}/\delta\le4V^{1-\delta}/\delta$.

(b) For $\frac14\le\sigma\le2$ apply (a) with $\delta=\frac14$: $|\zeta(s)|\le C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\le C_{1/4}T^{11/8}$. For $-\frac58\le\sigma\le\frac14$, $\re(1-s)\in[\frac34,\frac{13}8]$, so (a) with $\delta=\frac34$ and \cref{quoted:mv} give $|\zeta(s)|\le c_{\mathrm{MV}}(3T)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\le3^{9/8}c_{\mathrm{MV}}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}$, using $T+4\le3T$ and $\frac14\le\frac12-\sigma\le\frac98$. Finally, $\re(2s+2)\in[\frac34,6]$ and $|\im(2s+2)|=2T\ge4$, so (a) with $\delta=\frac34$ applies.
\end{proof}

203	and $hv_h^d\le x/\kappa_1$ bounds the last term by $\kappa_2^2xv_h^{d-1}/((2d-1)\kappa_1)$. For $d=1$, $f''=0$ and $\int_z^{v_h}|F_h'|\le h\kappa_2^2v_h\le\kappa_2^2x/\kappa_1$.
204	\end{proof}
205	
206	\begin{proof}[Proof of \eqref{eq:avg2}]
207	\emph{Truncation in $r$.} Put
208	\[
209	\Sing_R(n)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\frac{c_r(n)}{\varphi(r)},\qquad W_R(h)=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\beta_r(h).
210	\]
211	By \cref{prop:ramanujan-sing,lem:W-ident} and the bounds $|c_r(n)|\le\varphi(r)$ and $|\beta_r(h)|\le1$,
212	\[
213	|\Sing(n)-\Sing_R(n)|\le\mathcal T(R),\qquad|W_f(h)-W_R(h)|\le\mathcal T(R)
214	\]
215	uniformly in $n,h$. Let $M_R$ and $I_R$ be $M_f$ and $I_f$ with $\Sing$ and $W_f$ replaced by $\Sing_R$ and $W_R$. For fixed $k$ there are at most $x/f(k)$ values of $h$, each with $0\le x-hf(k)\le x$, so by \eqref{eq:sum-w}
216	\[
217	|M_f-M_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\sum_{z<k\le y}\frac{f'(k)}{f(k)}\le2U\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x).
218	\]
219	Similarly, for each $t\in[Z,Y]$ there are at most $x/t$ values of $h$, so $|I_f-I_R|\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\int_Z^Y\dd t/t\le\mathcal T(R)x^2\log(2x)$.
220	
221	\emph{The finite approximations.} All remaining sums are finite and may be rearranged. For integers $k\in(z,y]$, the condition $h\le x/f(k)$ is equivalent to $k\le v_h$, and $k>z$ forces $h<x/Z$. Hence
222	\[
223	M_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\sum_{z<k\le v_h}F_h(k)\frac{c_r(hf(k))}{\varphi(r)}.
224	\]
225	The sequence $k\mapsto c_r(hf(k))/\varphi(r)$ has period $r$, because $f$ has integer coefficients, and its mean is $\beta_r(h)$. The substitution $t=f(u)$ gives
226	\[
227	\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u=\int_Z^{\min\{Y,x/h\}}(x-ht)\dd t,
228	\]
229	and therefore $I_R=\sum_{r\le R}\lambda(r)\sum_{h\le H_0}\beta_r(h)\int_z^{v_h}F_h(u)\dd u$. By \cref{lem:periodic,lem:weight-var}, the inner difference for fixed $r$ and $h$ is at most $4rK_2xv_h^{d-1}\le4rK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}x^{2-1/d}h^{-1+1/d}$. If $v_h=z$ the difference is zero. By \cref{lem:sums}(e), $\sum_{h\le H_0}h^{-1+1/d}\le d(x/Z)^{1/d}$, so for fixed $r$ the total difference is at most $K_3rx^2Z^{-1/d}$ with $K_3=4dK_2\kappa_1^{-(d-1)/d}$. No logarithm arises here. Multiplying by $\lambda(r)$ and summing over $r\le R$ gives
230	\[
231	|M_R-I_R|\le K_3x^2Z^{-1/d}\mathcal N(R).
232	\]
233	
234	Combining the three estimates proves
235	\[
236	|M_f-I_f|\le C_0x^2\Bigl(K_3Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}(\log2R)^2+(2U+1)R^{-1/2}(\log2R)^2\log(2x)\Bigr).
237	\]
238	Together with the first part, \cref{prop:averaging} holds with $C(f)=C_0\max\{4D_w\kappa_2^{1/d},K_3,2U+1\}$.
239	\end{proof}

241	\begin{remark}
242	The error $x^2Z^{-1/d}R^{1/2}$ comes from the $k$-sampling of a weight of total variation about $xv_h^{d-1}$, summed over $h$ with the $h$-dependent endpoint $v_h$. The archived plan points out that using the endpoint $y$ for every $h$, instead of $v_h$, would lose the claimed range. The error is small only when $Z^{1/d}$, which is comparable to $z$, is large compared with $R$. Balancing this error against the tail $R^{-1/2}$ leads to the choice $R=Z^{1/d}$ in \cref{ch:assembly}.
243	\end{remark}
244	\chapter{The Dirichlet series of the averaged singular series}\label{ch:dirichlet}
245	
246	The averaged singular series $W_f(h)$ is a product of local factors that depend only on whether $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. Its Dirichlet series therefore factors as $\zeta(s)$ times an Euler product, and a second factorisation exhibits a pole of $\zeta(2s+2)$ at $s=-\frac12$. This pole, which is invisible in the region of absolute convergence, produces the main term of \cref{thm:main}. (Archived source: proposition P5, a crux of the plan.)
247	
248	\section{Facts about the zeta function}
249	
250	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta}
251	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
252	\item For every integer $N\ge1$ and $\re w>0$, $w\ne1$,
253	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-N}
254	\zeta(w)=\sum_{n\le N}n^{-w}+\frac{N^{1-w}}{w-1}-w\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-w-1}\dd u.
255	\end{equation}
256	In $\re w>0$ the only pole of $\zeta$ is a simple pole at $w=1$ with residue $1$, and $\lim_{w\to1}\bigl(\zeta(w)-\frac1{w-1}\bigr)=\gamma_E$, Euler's constant.
257	\item Let $\mathcal B_2(u)=\{u\}^2-\{u\}+\frac16$. The formula
258	\begin{equation}\label{eq:zeta-B2}
259	\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12+\frac w{12}-\frac{w(w+1)}2\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u
260	\end{equation}
261	continues $\zeta$ meromorphically to $\re w>-1$, with the single pole at $w=1$. In particular $\zeta(0)=-\frac12$ and $-\frac14\le\zeta(-\frac12)\le-\frac16$.
262	\end{enumerate}
263	\end{lemma}
264	
265	\begin{proof}
266	(a) For $\re w>1$ write $\sum_{n>N}n^{-w}=\int_N^\infty u^{-w}\dd\lfloor u\rfloor$, replace $\lfloor u\rfloor=u-\{u\}$, and integrate the second part by parts; the boundary term at $N$ vanishes because $\{N\}=0$. This gives \eqref{eq:zeta-N}. The integral converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $\re w>0$ because $0\le\{u\}<1$, which gives the continuation and the description of the pole. Subtracting $1/(w-1)$ and letting $w\to1$ gives $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N-\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-2}\dd u$. The integral lies in $[0,1/N]$, and letting $N\to\infty$ gives $\gamma_E$ by its definition as $\lim(\sum_{n\le N}n^{-1}-\log N)$.
267	
268	(b) With $N=1$, \eqref{eq:zeta-N} becomes $\zeta(w)=\frac1{w-1}+\frac12-w\int_1^\infty(\{u\}-\frac12)u^{-w-1}\dd u$. The function $\mathcal B_2$ is continuous, satisfies $|\mathcal B_2|\le\frac16$, and has derivative $2(\{u\}-\frac12)$ between integers. Integration by parts over $[1,T]$ for integers $T\ge2$ gives
269	\[
270	\int_1^T\Bigl(\{u\}-\frac12\Bigr)u^{-w-1}\dd u=\frac{T^{-w-1}-1}{12}+\frac{w+1}2\int_1^T\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-w-2}\dd u,
271	\]
272	and letting $T\to\infty$ for $\re w>1$ yields \eqref{eq:zeta-B2}. The last integral and its $w$-derivatives are dominated on $\re w\ge\eta>-1$ by $(\log u)^mu^{-\eta-2}/6$, so the integral is holomorphic for $\re w>-1$. At $w=0$ the formula gives $-1+\frac12=-\frac12$. At $w=-\frac12$ it gives $\zeta(-\frac12)=-\frac5{24}+\frac18\int_1^\infty\mathcal B_2(u)u^{-3/2}\dd u$, and the integral has modulus at most $\frac16\cdot2=\frac13$.
273	\end{proof}

275	\section{The local factors}
276	
277	For each prime $p$ put
278	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd}
279	\alpha_p=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
280	\beta_p=\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4},\qquad
281	\delta_p=\frac1{p^2}-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}.
282	\end{equation}
283	By \eqref{eq:W-intro}, $w_p(h)$ equals $\alpha_p$, $\alpha_p+\beta_p$ or $\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p$ according as $p\nmid h$, $p\parallel h$ or $p^2\mid h$. By \cref{lem:rho} (with $C_0=\max\{d,|A_d|\}$),
284	\begin{equation}\label{eq:abd-bounds}
285	1-\frac2{p^2}\le\alpha_p\le1,\quad0\le\beta_p\le\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}\le\frac{C_0}{p^3},\quad0\le\delta_p\le\frac1{p^2},\quad\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-\frac1{p^2}.
286	\end{equation}
287	Here $\beta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p\rho(p)$, $\delta_p\ge0$ because $\rho(p)\le p$, and $\alpha_p\le1$ because $\rho(p^2)\le p^2$. Define
288	\begin{equation}\label{eq:LM}
289	L_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pp^{-s}+\delta_pp^{-2s},\qquad
290	M_p(s)=\bigl(1-p^{-2s-2}\bigr)L_p(s),
291	\end{equation}
292	and $P_f(s)=\prod_pL_p(s)$, $H_f(s)=\prod_pM_p(s)$. In the notation of the archived proposition, $L_p(s)=(1-2p^{-2})B_p(s)$ with $B_p(s)=a_p+(b_p-a_p)p^{-s}+(c_p-b_p)p^{-2s}$, $a_p=1+\rho(p^2)/(p^2(p^2-2))$, $b_p=1+\rho(p)/(p(p^2-2))$, $c_p=1+1/(p^2-2)$. Expanding the product, with $z=p^{-s}$,
293	\begin{equation}\label{eq:M-expand}
294	M_p(s)=\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\bigl(\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}\bigr)z^2-\beta_pp^{-2}z^3-\delta_pp^{-2}z^4,\qquad
295	\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}=-\frac{\rho(p)}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^6}.
296	\end{equation}
297	The cancellation of the terms $\pm p^{-2}$ in the coefficient of $z^2$ is what allows $H_f$ to converge beyond $\re s=-\frac12$.
298	
299	\section{The factorisation}
300	
301	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Df}
302	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
303	\item The series $D_f(s)=\sum_hW_f(h)h^{-s}$ converges absolutely for $\re s>1$.
304	\item The products $P_f$ and $H_f$ converge absolutely and locally uniformly, and define holomorphic functions, on $\re s>-\frac12$ and $\re s>-\frac34$ respectively. For every fixed $\sigma>-\frac34$ there is $C(f,\sigma)$ with $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le C(f,\sigma)$ for all real $t$.
305	\item For $\re s>1$, $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. The function $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ continues $D_f$ meromorphically to $\re s>-\frac34$, and its only possible poles there are simple poles at $s=1$ and $s=-\frac12$.
306	\item $R_f=\Res_{s=1}D_f(s)=P_f(1)$. Moreover $R_f=\widetilde R_f$, where $\widetilde R_f$ is the series of \cref{lem:W-basic}, and \eqref{eq:R-intro} holds. Moreover $B_f=(\gamma_E-\frac32)R_f+P_f'(1)$, and $R_f>0$.
307	\item $D_f(0)=-\frac1{2\zeta(2)}=-\frac c2$.
308	\item We have $\Res_{s=-1/2}D_f(s)=\frac12\zeta(-\frac12)H_f(-\frac12)$, and hence
309	\[
310	K_f=-\tfrac83\,\zeta(-\tfrac12)\,H_f(-\tfrac12).
311	\]
312	Moreover $H_f(-\frac12)>0$ and $K_f>0$, and $K_f$ is given by the absolutely convergent product \eqref{eq:K-intro}.
313	\end{enumerate}
314	\end{proposition}
315	
316	\begin{proof}
317	(a) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $0<W_f(h)\le1$, so $\sum_h|W_f(h)h^{-s}|\le\sum_hh^{-\re s}$.
318	
319	(b) For $\re s\ge\sigma$, \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} gives $|L_p(s)-1|\le2p^{-2}+C_0p^{-3-\sigma}+p^{-2-2\sigma}$. If $\sigma>-\frac12$ all exponents exceed one, so by \cref{lem:sums}(c) the sum over $p$ converges uniformly on $\re s\ge\sigma$, and \cref{lem:products} applies. For $M_p$, \eqref{eq:M-expand} and \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} give, for $\re s\ge\sigma$,
320	\[
321	|M_p(s)-1|\le\frac2{p^2}+\frac{C_0}{p^{3+\sigma}}+\Bigl(\frac{C_0}{p^3}+\frac2{p^4}+\frac{C_0}{p^5}\Bigr)p^{-2\sigma}+\frac{C_0}{p^{5+3\sigma}}+\frac1{p^{4+4\sigma}}.
322	\]
323	For $\sigma>-\frac34$ the exponents $2$, $3+\sigma$, $3+2\sigma$, $4+2\sigma$, $5+2\sigma$, $5+3\sigma$ and $4+4\sigma$ all exceed one. Hence $\sum_p\sup_{\re s\ge\sigma}|M_p(s)-1|=:E_H(\sigma)<\infty$, and \cref{lem:products} gives absolute and locally uniform convergence, holomorphy, and $|H_f(\sigma+it)|\le\exp(E_H(\sigma))$ for all $t$.
324	
325	(c) By \cref{lem:W-basic}, $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p>0$, and $u(h)=W_f(h)/W_f(1)$ is multiplicative with $u(p)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p)/\alpha_p$ and $u(p^e)=(\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p)/\alpha_p$ for $e\ge2$. For $\re s>1$ and $z=p^{-s}$ its local series is
326	\[
327	1+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p}{\alpha_p}z+\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p}{\alpha_p}\cdot\frac{z^2}{1-z}=\frac{\alpha_p+\beta_pz+\delta_pz^2}{\alpha_p(1-z)}=\frac{L_p(s)}{\alpha_p(1-p^{-s})}.
328	\]
329	Since $\sum_h|u(h)h^{-s}|<\infty$, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\sum_hu(h)h^{-s}=\prod_pL_p(s)\alpha_p^{-1}(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. Multiplying by the convergent product $W_f(1)=\prod_p\alpha_p$ and using the Euler product of $\zeta$ gives $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)P_f(s)$; the limits of partial products multiply. For $\re s>-\frac12$ we have $\re(2s+2)>1$, so $\prod_p(1-p^{-2s-2})^{-1}=\zeta(2s+2)$ converges absolutely, and multiplying the products gives $P_f(s)=\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$. By \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $\zeta(s)$ and $\zeta(2s+2)$ are meromorphic for $\re s>-\frac34$, since then $\re s>-1$ and $\re(2s+2)>\frac12$. Their only poles there are at $s=1$ and at $2s+2=1$, both simple. Since $H_f$ is holomorphic, $\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ is the required continuation.
330	
331	(d) Since $P_f$ is holomorphic near $1$ and $\zeta(s)=\frac1{s-1}+\gamma_E+O(s-1)$ by \cref{lem:zeta}(a), we have $D_f(s)=\frac{P_f(1)}{s-1}+\gamma_EP_f(1)+P_f'(1)+O(s-1)$. This gives $R_f=P_f(1)$ and the formula for $B_f$ from \eqref{eq:RBK}. Substituting \eqref{eq:abd},
332	\[
333	L_p(1)=\alpha_p+\frac{\beta_p}p+\frac{\delta_p}{p^2}=1-\frac2{p^2}+\frac1{p^4}+\frac{(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))}{p^4}
334	=\Bigl(1-\frac1{p^2}\Bigr)^2\bigl(1+T_p\bigr),
335	\]
336	with $T_p=(1-1/p)(\rho(p)+\rho(p^2))/(p^2-1)^2\ge0$. By \cref{lem:rho}(d) and $p^2-1\ge\frac34p^2$, $T_p\le\frac{16C_0}9(p^{-3}+p^{-4})$, which is summable. Using \eqref{eq:c-euler}, $R_f=\zeta(2)^{-2}\prod_p(1+T_p)>0$, which is \eqref{eq:R-intro}. For the identification with $\widetilde R_f$, note that $\lambda(r)\rho(r)/r=c^2v(r)$, where $v$ is the nonnegative multiplicative function supported on cube-free integers with
337	\[
338	v(p)=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p)}{(p^2-1)^2},\qquad v(p^2)=\frac{\varphi(p^2)\rho(p^2)}{p^2(p^2-1)^2}=\frac{(1-1/p)\rho(p^2)}{(p^2-1)^2},
339	\]
340	using \cref{lem:rho}(a) for multiplicativity of $\rho$. Thus $1+v(p)+v(p^2)=1+T_p$. Since $\sum_rv(r)<\infty$ by \cref{lem:W-basic}, \cref{lem:euler} gives $\widetilde R_f=c^2\prod_p(1+T_p)=R_f$.
341	
342	(e) $L_p(0)=\alpha_p+\beta_p+\delta_p=1-p^{-2}$, so $P_f(0)=c$ by \eqref{eq:c-euler}. The identity $D_f=\zeta P_f$ persists on $\re s>-\frac12$ by (c), and both factors are regular at $0$; by \cref{lem:zeta}(b), $D_f(0)=\zeta(0)c=-c/2$.
343	
344	(f) Near $s=-\frac12$, $\zeta(2s+2)=\frac{1/2}{s+1/2}+O(1)$, while $\zeta(s)$ and $H_f(s)$ are holomorphic. This gives the residue, and the formula for $K_f$ follows from \eqref{eq:RBK}. At $s=-\frac12$,
345	\[
346	M_p(-\tfrac12)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\bigl(\alpha_p+\beta_p\sqrt p+\delta_pp\bigr)=\Bigl(1-\frac1p\Bigr)\Bigl(1+\frac1p-\frac{2+\rho(p)}{p^2}+\frac{\rho(p)}{p^{5/2}}-\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^{7/2}}+\frac{\rho(p^2)}{p^4}\Bigr),
347	\]
348	by direct substitution of \eqref{eq:abd}. This is positive because $\alpha_p>0$ and $\beta_p,\delta_p\ge0$. The deviations $|M_p(-\frac12)-1|$ are summable by (b), so \cref{lem:products}(c) gives $H_f(-\frac12)>0$, and \cref{lem:zeta}(b) gives $\zeta(-\frac12)<0$. Hence $K_f>0$, and \eqref{eq:K-intro} is the product $H_f(-\frac12)=\prod_pM_p(-\frac12)$, with the factors at each prime kept together.
349	\end{proof}
350	
351	\begin{remark}
352	Both poles in (c) are genuine, since $R_f>0$ and $K_f>0$. The value $D_f(0)=-c/2$ is essential: in \cref{ch:mellin} it produces the term $+cH$ in the expansion of $\Theta_f(H)$, which cancels the diagonal term $cx(Y-Z)$ of \cref{prop:reduction}. 362	\section{Growth in a vertical strip}
363	
364	We need one result from the literature. It is a consequence of the functional equation $\zeta(s)=\zeta(1-s)2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\sin(\pi s/2)$ \cite[Corollary~10.4]{montgomeryvaughan2007} and Stirling's formula.
365	
366	\begin{quoted}[{\cite[Corollary~10.5]{montgomeryvaughan2007}}]\label{quoted:mv}
367	Suppose that $A>0$ is fixed. Then $|\zeta(s)|\asymp\tau^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|$ uniformly for $|\sigma|\le A$ and $|t|\ge1$. Here $s=\sigma+it$ and $\tau=|t|+4$.
368	\end{quoted}
369	
370	We use it with $A=2$, only for $-\frac58\le\sigma\le\frac14$ and $|t|\ge2$. Let $c_{\mathrm{MV}}$ be a constant for the upper inequality there, so that $|\zeta(s)|\le c_{\mathrm{MV}}(|t|+4)^{1/2-\sigma}|\zeta(1-s)|$. No conditional estimate for $\zeta$ is used. (The holomorphy of $\zeta$ in the strip away from $s=1$ is already contained in \cref{lem:zeta}(b).)
371	
372	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zeta-growth}
373	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
374	\item Let $\delta\in\{\frac14,\frac34\}$ and $C_\delta=(\frac32)^{1-\delta}\bigl(\frac1{1-\delta}+1\bigr)+\frac4\delta$. Then $|\zeta(\alpha+iv)|\le C_\delta|v|^{1-\delta}$ for $\delta\le\alpha\le6$ and $|v|\ge2$.
375	\item For $s=\sigma+it$ with $-\frac58\le\sigma\le2$ and $T=|t|\ge2$,
376	\[
377	|\zeta(s)|\le C_\zeta T^{11/8},\qquad|\zeta(2s+2)|\le C_{3/4}(2T)^{1/4},\qquad C_\zeta=\max\{C_{1/4},\,3^{9/8}c_{\mathrm{MV}}C_{3/4}\}.
378	\]
379	\end{enumerate}
380	\end{lemma}
381	
382	\begin{proof}
383	(a) Let $V=|v|$ and use \eqref{eq:zeta-N} with $N=\lceil V\rceil$, so $V\le N\le\frac32V$. The finite sum has modulus at most $\sum_{n\le N}n^{-\delta}\le N^{1-\delta}/(1-\delta)\le(\frac32)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}/(1-\delta)$. Next, $|N^{1-s}/(s-1)|\le N^{1-\delta}/V\le(\frac32)^{1-\delta}V^{1-\delta}$. Finally $|s\int_N^\infty\{u\}u^{-s-1}\dd u|\le|s|N^{-\alpha}/\alpha\le(V+6)V^{-\delta}/\delta\le4V^{1-\delta}/\delta$.
384	
385	(b) For $\frac14\le\sigma\le2$ apply (a) with $\delta=\frac14$: $|\zeta(s)|\le C_{1/4}T^{3/4}\le C_{1/4}T^{11/8}$. For $-\frac58\le\sigma\le\frac14$, $\re(1-s)\in[\frac34,\frac{13}8]$, so (a) with $\delta=\frac34$ and \cref{quoted:mv} give $|\zeta(s)|\le c_{\mathrm{MV}}(3T)^{1/2-\sigma}C_{3/4}T^{1/4}\le3^{9/8}c_{\mathrm{MV}}C_{3/4}T^{11/8}$, using $T+4\le3T$ and $\frac14\le\frac12-\sigma\le\frac98$. Finally, $\re(2s+2)\in[\frac34,6]$ and $|\im(2s+2)|=2T\ge4$, so (a) with $\delta=\frac34$ applies.
386	\end{proof}
387	
388	The bound of \cref{prop:Df}(b) for $H_f$ holds on each vertical line, but the contour shift needs a bound that is uniform on a strip. The archived proof supplies it directly from the Euler product.
389	
390	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:H-strip}
391	Let $\mathcal B$ be the finite set of primes dividing every coefficient of $f$. For $-\frac58\le\re s\le2$,
392	\[
393	|H_f(s)|\le M_H:=e^{8(1+d)}\prod_{p\in\mathcal B}\bigl(1+p^{-3/4}\bigr)\bigl(1+p^{5/8}+p^{5/4}\bigr).
394	\]
395	Consequently, with $C_D=2^{1/4}M_HC_\zeta C_{3/4}$,
396	\begin{equation}\label{eq:D-growth}
397	|D_f(\sigma+it)|\le C_D|t|^{13/8}\qquad\bigl(-\tfrac58\le\sigma\le2,\ |t|\ge2\bigr).
398	\end{equation}
399	\end{lemma}
400	
401	\begin{proof}
402	Let $z=p^{-s}$, so $|z|\le p^{5/8}$. For $p\notin\mathcal B$, \cref{lem:rho}(c) gives $\rho(p)\le d$ and $\rho(p^2)\le dp$. Together with \eqref{eq:abd-bounds} this yields $|\alpha_p-1|\le2p^{-2}$, $\beta_p\le dp^{-3}$, $\delta_p\le p^{-2}$ and $|\delta_p-\alpha_pp^{-2}|\le dp^{-3}+2p^{-4}+dp^{-5}\le(2d+1)p^{-3}$. By \eqref{eq:M-expand},
403	\[
404	|M_p(s)-1|\le2p^{-2}+dp^{-19/8}+(2d+1)p^{-7/4}+dp^{-25/8}+p^{-3/2}\le(4+4d)p^{-3/2},
405	\]
406	and $\sum_p(4+4d)p^{-3/2}\le(4+4d)\int_1^\infty u^{-3/2}\dd u=8(1+d)$. Hence $|\prod_{p\notin\mathcal B}M_p(s)|\le\prod(1+|M_p(s)-1|)\le e^{8(1+d)}$. For the finitely many $p\in\mathcal B$ use $0\le\alpha_p,\beta_p,\delta_p\le1$ to get $|M_p(s)|\le(1+p^{-2}|z|^2)(1+|z|+|z|^2)\le(1+p^{-3/4})(1+p^{5/8}+p^{5/4})$. The bound \eqref{eq:D-growth} then follows from $D_f(s)=\zeta(s)\zeta(2s+2)H_f(s)$ and \cref{lem:zeta-growth}(b).
407	\end{proof}
408	
409	\section{The Mellin representation}
410	
411	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:kernel}
412	For real $v>0$,
413	\[
414	\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{1-i\infty}^{1+i\infty}\frac{2v^z}{z(z+1)(z+2)}\dd z=\begin{cases}(1-v^{-1})^2,&v\ge1,\\0,&0<v<1.\end{cases}
415	\]
416	\end{lemma}
417	
418	\begin{proof}
419	The integral converges absolutely. For $v\ge1$, close the contour by a rectangle to the left, with horizontal sides at heights $\pm T$ and a left side on $\re z=-N-\frac12$ with an integer $N\ge3$. On the horizontal sides the integrand is $O_v(T^{-3})$, so their contribution tends to zero as $T\to\infty$. On the left side each of $|z|,|z+1|,|z+2|$ is at least $\sqrt{(N-3/2)^2+(\im z)^2}$, so the normalised integral is at most $\frac{v^{-N-1/2}}\pi\int_{\R}((N-\frac32)^2+t^2)^{-3/2}\dd t=\frac{2v^{-N-1/2}}{\pi(N-3/2)^2}$, which tends to zero also when $v=1$. The residues at $z=0,-1,-2$ are $1$, $-2v^{-1}$ and $v^{-2}$, with sum $(1-v^{-1})^2$. For $v<1$, close to the right instead; the right side $\re z=N$ contributes at most $2v^N/(\pi N^2)\to0$, and there are no poles.
420	\end{proof}
421	
422	\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Theta}
423	There is $C(f)>0$ such that, uniformly for real $H\ge1$,
424	\begin{equation}\label{eq:Theta}
425	\Bigl|\Theta_f(H)-\bigl(R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2+cH-K_fH^{1/2}\bigr)\Bigr|\le C(f)H^{3/8},
426	\end{equation}
427	and consequently
428	\begin{equation}\label{eq:F-asym}
429	\bigl|F_f(H)-K_fH^{-3/2}\bigr|\le C(f)H^{-13/8},\qquad|F_f(H)|\le(K_f+C(f))H^{-3/2}.
430	\end{equation}
431	\end{proposition}
432	
433	\begin{proof}
434	\emph{Mellin representation.} Apply \cref{lem:kernel} with $v=H/h$, multiply by $H^2W_f(h)/h$ and sum over $h\ge1$; note $H^2(1-h/H)^2=(H-h)^2$, and a term with $h=H$ vanishes on both sides. With $s=z+1$ the integrand becomes $2W_f(h)H^{s+1}h^{-s}/((s-1)s(s+1))$ on $\re s=2$. The sum over $h$ of its absolute values is at most $2H^3\zeta(2)/|(s-1)s(s+1)|$, which is integrable on the line, because $|(s-1)s(s+1)|\ge|\im s|^3$ there and the denominator does not vanish. Hence summation and integration may be interchanged, and
435	\[
436	\Theta_f(H)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{2-i\infty}^{2+i\infty}G_H(s)\dd s,\qquad G_H(s)=\frac{2D_f(s)H^{s+1}}{(s-1)s(s+1)}.
437	\]
438	
439	\emph{Contour shift.} In the strip $-\frac58\le\re s\le2$ the poles of $G_H$ are at $s=1$ and $s=-\frac12$ (from $D_f$, \cref{prop:Df}(c)) and at $s=0$ (from the kernel); the pole of the kernel at $-1$ lies outside. On the horizontal segments at height $\pm T$, $T\ge2$, each factor of the denominator has modulus at least $T$, and $|H^{s+1}|\le H^3$. So \eqref{eq:D-growth} bounds the integrand by $2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}$. The segments have length $\frac{21}8$, so their total contribution is at most $\frac{21}2C_DH^3T^{-11/8}\to0$ as $T\to\infty$, for each fixed $H$. On the line $\re s=-\frac58$ we have $|(s-1)s(s+1)|\ge\frac{13}8\cdot\frac58\cdot\frac38=\frac{195}{512}$. With $M_0=\max_{|t|\le2}|D_f(-\frac58+it)|$, finite because the line contains no pole, the part $|t|\le2$ contributes at most $4\cdot\frac{512}{195}\cdot2M_0H^{3/8}$ to the integral of $|G_H|$. For $|t|\ge2$, \eqref{eq:D-growth} gives $|G_H|\le2C_DH^{3/8}|t|^{-11/8}$, and these tails contribute at most $4C_DH^{3/8}\int_2^\infty t^{-11/8}\dd t=\frac{32}3C_D2^{-3/8}H^{3/8}$. Hence the residue theorem gives
440	\[
441	\Theta_f(H)=\sum_{s_0\in\{1,0,-1/2\}}\Res_{s=s_0}G_H(s)+E_f(H),\qquad|E_f(H)|\le C_*H^{3/8},
442	\]
443	where $C_*=\frac1{2\pi}\bigl(\frac{4096}{195}M_0+\frac{32}3C_D2^{-3/8}\bigr)$ depends only on $f$.
444	
445	\emph{Residues.} Write $D_f(s)=\frac{R_f}{s-1}+L_f+O(s-1)$ near $s=1$, so that $B_f=L_f-\frac32R_f$ by \eqref{eq:RBK}, and put $q(s)=2/(s(s+1))$. Then $q(1)=1$ and $q'(1)=-\frac32$, and $G_H(s)=q(s)H^{s+1}D_f(s)/(s-1)$ has the residue
446	\begin{align*}
447	\Res_{s=1}G_H&=R_f\frac{\dd}{\dd s}\bigl(q(s)H^{s+1}\bigr)\Big|_{s=1}+L_fq(1)H^2\\
448	&=H^2\bigl(R_f\log H-\tfrac32R_f+L_f\bigr)=R_fH^2\log H+B_fH^2.
449	\end{align*}
450	At $s=0$, \cref{prop:Df}(e) gives
451	\[
452	\Res_{s=0}G_H=\frac{2D_f(0)H}{(-1)\cdot1}=-2D_f(0)H=cH.
453	\]
454	At $s=-\frac12$ the denominator equals $(-\frac32)(-\frac12)(\frac12)=\frac38$, so by \eqref{eq:RBK}
455	\[
456	\Res_{s=-1/2}G_H=\frac{16}3H^{1/2}\Res_{s=-1/2}D_f=-K_fH^{1/2}.
457	\]
458	
459	This proves \eqref{eq:Theta} with $C(f)=1+C_*$, for every real $H\ge1$, integral or not. Substituting into \eqref{eq:ThetaF} gives the exact identity $F_f(H)=K_fH^{-3/2}-E_f(H)/H^2$, which implies \eqref{eq:F-asym} since $H^{-13/8}\le H^{-3/2}$.
460	\end{proof}
461	
462	\section{The integral identity}
463	
464	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:integral-identity}
465	For real $x\ge2$ and $2\le Z\le Y\le x$,
466	\[
467	2\int_Z^Y\sum_{1\le h\le x/t}(x-ht)W_f(h)\dd t=Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)-Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y).
468	\]
469	\end{lemma}
470	
471	\begin{proof}
472	Write $u_+=\max\{u,0\}$. For $t\in[Z,Y]$ only $h\le x/Z$ contribute, so the left side equals $\sum_{h\le x/Z}W_f(h)\cdot2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\dd t$. The function $t\mapsto(x-ht)_+^2$ is continuously differentiable with derivative $-2h(x-ht)_+$, hence $2\int_Z^Y(x-ht)_+\dd t=\bigl((x-hZ)_+^2-(x-hY)_+^2\bigr)/h$. On the other hand, by the definition of $\Theta_f$, $Z^2\Theta_f(x/Z)=\sum_{h\le x/Z}W_f(h)(x-hZ)_+^2/h$ and $Y^2\Theta_f(x/Y)=\sum_{h\le x/Z}W_f(h)(x-hY)_+^2/h$; in the second sum the terms with $h>x/Y$ vanish. Subtracting gives the identity, with no error term. Note that $x/Z,x/Y\ge1$.
473	\end{proof}
